summary: The assessee, a Hindu Undivided Family, was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66 and 1966 67. In respect of certain assets, he claimed that the income from the property should be included in his net wealth as it had been acquired by him during the previous year. The Wealth Tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the assessee had not furnished any return or evidence to show that the asset was acquired by the assessee during the relevant period. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the Wealth Tax officer was justified in including the value of the assets of the assessee under section 7 (1) of the Act. On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal confirmed the order of the Income Tax Officer. The High Court affirmed the view taken by the Tribunal. Dismis sing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The expression " net wealth " is defined by cl. (m) of s. 2 of the Wealth tax Act, 1957. [ 310 B ] 2. The definition of the term " net Wealth " in clause (q) of section 2 of that Act is wide enough to include all the assets which are capable of being used for the purpose of earning income. The assets are not confined to cash, its value is determined pursuant to sub section (I) of Section 7 as the estimated price, which in the opinion of the wealth tax Officer, the asset would fetch if sold in the open market on the valuation date. [ 311 C D ] 3. The value of a property is determined based upon the total value of all the debts owed by the asses ee on the basis of the value determined under sub section 1 of section 7 as also the amount of the net wealth of the person liable to pay tax. [ 312 F G ] 4. The principle underlying the provisions of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, is that the value should be determined as on the date of the valuation. [ 313 E ] 5. The computation of the gross wealth of an assessee has to be done on the last day of the previous years. If the asset is an asset other than cash, it is the value which is determined under the Income tax Act. [ 314 A B ] 6. The method of accounting adopted by the appellant is not correct. It is apparent that what accrues as a right also falls to be included within the assets.

The respondent was a Government servant. He was charged with the misconduct of having committed an act of misconduct in his capacity as a public servant and he was convicted by the criminal court for the offence under section 120 B IPC. The Tribunal found that the respondent had committed an offence punishable under section 13 (2) read with Section 5 (1)( d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and sentenced him to pay a fine of Rs. 6, 000 / and in default to undergo simple imprisonment for one year. In appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the penalty imposed upon him was disproportionate to the charge proved against him and that the High Court erred in holding that the punishment awarded to him was too harsh. Dismis sing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The penalty imposed by the disciplinary authority is not excessive or grossly disproportionate to t he gravity of the charges. [ 10 D ] 2. The respondent has been found guilty of the charge framed against him. He has also been found to be guilty of misconduct. The finding of the Inquiry Officer that the delinquent was guilty of mis de mean our is based on the evidence adduced during the course of the enquiry. The findings are not perverse. The conclusion arrived at by the Inquiry officer is not vitiated by any error of law or fact. [ 11 E F ] 3. The order of the Disciplinary Authority imposing the penalty is bad in law. It cannot be sustained. [ 12 G H; 12 A ] 4. The High Court has rightly set aside the order of dismissal passed by the Disciplinary authority.

The appellant, a tenant of the respondent landlord filed a suit for eviction against the respondent on the ground that he was a trespasser in respect of certain lands in question. The Trial Court decreed the suit and directed the respondent to vacate the premises. In appeal, the High Court held that the respondent had not been evicted from the land on the basis of the decree passed by the Civil Court and dismissed the suit. On further appeal, it was contended that the suit was barred by res judicata as well as constructive res judicata. Allow ing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court has rightly held that there is no bar under section 7 (2) of the Act to entertain the suit for recovery of possession of the land of which the respondent is a tenant or a deemed tenant under the Act. [ 10 31 F ] 2. The provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure are applicable to the proceedings before the Civil Courts. Section 8 (2), however, provides that where any person is a deemed tenants under the provisions of an Act, the Mamlatdar shall take action to determine whether such person is or is not a tenant under that Act. It would be just and fair if the procedure laid down in Order 7 Rules 10 and 10A of the CPC is followed. [ 1032 B C ] 3. The object underlying the provision is to prevent the mischief of the legislature. If the Legislature intended to give relief to persons who were not parties to the suit, it would have provided for the same. But in order to avoid multiplicity of litigation, the Legislature has made a provision in the Act providing that the Civil court shall not have jurisdiction to settle, decide or deal with any question which is required to be settled, decided or dealt with by the Mamlatdar under the statute. [ 1033 E G ] 4. The expression " other than a person " occurring in section 8 (1) of Act is wide enough to include a person who is a non tenant or whose case is not governed by the Act but is covered by the provisions contained in the said Act. The words " any person " in section 2 (i) of that Act are wide enough and must be given their ordinary meaning. [ 1034 D E ] 5. The word'person'in section 7 of the Bombay Tenancy Act, 1908 means a person holding land under a tenure holder. The definition of'tenant'in the Bombay Land Revenue Code, 18 79 does not apply to the present case because the word'tenant ', in the context of the definition of the term'tenant '. [ 1034 H; 10 35 A ] 6. The Act is a beneficial legislation enacted to protect the interests of the tenants and to provide for the protection of the interest of the landlords. The Rent Act is not meant to be used as a sh ield to evict the tenants. The purpose of the enactment is to protect tenants from eviction and to ensure that they are not put in possession of any land or dwelling house held by them.

The petitioners are working as car p enters in the Corporation. They were employed by a company incorporated under the, and were paid wages at the rate of Rs. 1, 000 per month. In the year 1986, they were given the work of " A " class of employees. On account of the fact that the petitioners were not paid their wages for similar work, they filed a writ petition before this Court challenging the action of the respondents. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the petitioner was entitled to be regularised with effect from the date of his initial appointment. The petitioners challenged the order of the High Court in this Court. It was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the decision of the Government is arbitrary and violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. Dismis sing the petition, ^ HELD: (i) The principle of " equal pay for equal work " cannot be enforced. [ 669 G ] (ii) The doctrine of equal pay does not apply to the case of the petitioner. The principle that " equal work ", means " equal " or " equal ". The principle is applicable only to those who are employed in different establishments. The concept of equal work has been made applicable to all persons similarly situated. [ 670 B C ] (iii) The petitioners have no right to claim regularisation of their services. The distinction between the two categories of workers is not justified. The classification must be based on intelligible differentia which distinguish es them from other employees. [ 671 D E ] (iv) The classification has reasonable nexus with the object sought to be achieved. The differenti ation is not arbitrary but is based on some rational basis. [ 672 F ] (v) The discrimination complained of must be within the same est ab lish ment owned by the same management. [ 673 H; 674 A ] (vi) The equality claims of the employees are denied. The discrimination is not founded merely because there is a discrimination amongst the same set of employees by the very nature of job. [ 674 B ] (vii) The difference between the duties and responsibilities of the posts concerned is not a matter of mere mathe matical formula. It is not just a comparison of physical activity. It requires the consideration of various dimensions of the job. The quality of the work done cannot be the same as the job of the other employees in the same establishment. [ 676 C D ] (viii) The distinction drawn by the petitioners is not correct. The difference in the nature of work performed can be seen from the fact whether the petitioners'jobs are comparable with the counter parts in the government service. [ 677 C D ].

The prosecution case against accused 1 and 6 was that they had been falsely implicated in the murder of Mal an. Accused 2, 3 and 4 were tried for the mur ders of deceased Mal an and accused 5 and 7 by the Sessions Judge on the charge of conspiracy under section 302 read with section 120B I. P. C. and section 120B IPC. The trial court acquitted all the seven accused but convicted them under section 120 A read with sections 34 and 120B I I. PC. and sentenced each one of them to life imprisonment. On appeal by the State, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence awarded to the appellants. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) there was no evidence against the appellants; (ii) the appro ver's evidence was not reliable as he was not a party to the conspiracy; (iii) the evidence of the appro p ri ate witnesses was not sufficient to prove the guilt of the accused beyond all reasonable doubt; (iv) the confession of accused 6 was inadmissible in evidence because the prosecution did not examine any witness in support of its case; and (v) the confessional statement of accused 5 was not admissible in evidence as the same was retracted from his own statement. Dismis sing the appeal, HELD: (1) The confession of the appellant made before the police officer is not admissible under section 24 of the Evidence Act. [ 288 B ] (2) The confessional statement recorded by the police officers is admissible in law only if it is corroborated by other evidence. It is not necessary that the confession should be proved like any other fact. If the confession is voluntary and truthful, it is not possible to convict the accused merely on the basis of the confession. [ 289 D E ] (3) The evidence of appro ver P. W. 1 and the retracted confession of appellant 6 are not admissible as evidence in view of the provisions of section 30 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872. [ 290 G H ] (4) The extra judicial confession of co accused 6 cannot be relied upon unless it is supported by independent evidence. [ 291 F ] (5) The retracted confession is admissible under Section 27 of the Act. The confession is not substantive piece of evidence. The courts below have rightly held that the appro b ation of the said confession by the appro h ant is not reliable.

The appellant, a Hindu widow of the deceased, filed a suit for possession of certain properties on the ground that she was the owner of the properties mentioned in the will and that her husband had executed a will on August 31, 1946. She claimed to be entitled to the said properties as absolute owners under the will. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the suit holding that the will was not proved by the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court should have held that the document was not admissible in evidence because the testator had not been examined; and that the question whether the will had been duly proved or not must be decided in the present proceedings. Held: (i) The High Court was right in coming to the conclusion that the appellant's case was covered by section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act. It is well settled that where a document is produced in evidence without examining any person other than the attesting witness, the court has to decide the question of admissibility of such document in order to give effect to the terms of the document. If the court finds that the scribe was not competent to depose, the document cannot be admitted in evidence unless the person who made the statement was examined as a witness. (ii) The burden of proof is on the party who sets up the will to prove the due execution of the will, and if there are any suspicious circumstances surrounding the execution of it, the onus shifts on the prop ounder to remove the suspicion by clear and satisfactory evidence. (iii) The presumption of truth attached to an instrument is a weak one and the court may take into consideration all the relevant circumstances which appear from the evidence adduced before it. But it is not necessary that the court should look at all the circumstances of the case and decide upon the evidence in its entirety. (iv) The court has no power to reject the evidence of a witness merely because he is either a parti san or a parti ci ple of the opposite party or witnesses who are interested in the result of the litigation. Where the court is satisfied that the evidence given by the witness is wholly dis interested and unreliable, it would be safe to act upon it. In the instant case, the High C ourt was justified in reversing the finding of the trial court on the question about the character of the subsequent acquisitions of items 3, 4 and 5.

The appellants are manufacturers of electric energy in the State of Andhra Pradesh. They were assessed to sales tax for the period from April 1, 1956 to March 31, 1960 on the ground that they had not produced any account books or accounts for the purpose of showing that they were used as a part of a particular type of apparatus. The Sales Tax Officer held that the goods were covered by entry No. 4 and therefore liable to be taxed under Entry No. 6 of Schedule I of the Act. On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal held that it was not necessary to prove that the ar c carbon's were used in the process of welding electr odes but that the entry did not make any distinction between electrical appliances and apparatus which were used for the purposes of the business. In the appeals before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the entries in the schedule to the Act were not relevant to the question whether the ar cs were used exclusively for the use of the ar tis ans or other cin em as. Dismis sing the appeals, ^ HELD: (i) The entry in the Schedule is intended to cover only those parts which are used for a particular kind of instrument. It does not mean that all parts thereof should be used for some other purpose than what is actually used in connection with the main purpose. [ 563 B ] (ii) The expression " accessories " is used in a particular context in which it occurs. The word access ory is used to indicate the nature of the article itself. The term'accessories'is used as an aid or addition. A sense in which the word access ories is used is given in Web ster's Third New International Dictionary as follows: " all objects or device that is not essential in itself but that ad ds to the be a uty, convenience, or eff ecti veness of something else ". This is so because the word " accessories ", is used for an ancillary purpose. The same item may be an access ory of more than one kind of instruments. It will be noticed that the word'accessories ', is used when the word is used, in the context of the entry in question. [ 564 C D ] (iii) The words " parts thereof " are used in various entries such as entry No., 4. The expression'accessories " has been employed in the Act and the definition of'accessories '. The expression is used generally in the sense of'access ory '. The word'access'is defined in section 2 (e) of the General Clauses Act, 1897. The meaning of the word,'access ', is explained in the dictionary in the following manner: " Access ory means a thing which is used primarily for the specific purpose of the trade, and is not necessarily confined to particular machines for which it is used. The latter is used mainly for the production of electricity. The former is used solely for the manufacture of electric power ful light. The second is used by the legislature in the course of its business. The first entry is made in the year 1956. The last mentioned entry is in the form of a schedule to describe goods which may have been manufactured for use as an access ories. The entry is not restricted to certain items. The third entry is also not applicable to the case. The fourth entry is a residuary entry. The respondents are not entitled to claim exemption under the entry. [ 565 F H;

The petitioners are lessees of minor minerals in the State of Gujarat. They filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the validity of the Act and the Rules made thereunder. The High Court dismissed the petitions holding that the Act was not applicable to the petitioners as they were not holders of a mining lease or a mining leases. In appeal, this Court held that the levy of royalty under section 15 of the, is valid. Dismis sing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The power conferred by section 15 (2) of the Central Act is an enabling provision which confers on the State Government the power to make rules for regulating the grant of quarry leases, mining leases or other mineral concessions in respect of minor mineral. [ 409 G ] 2. The Act does not confer any power on the Central Government to make rule making provisions with regard to the grant or renewal of a quarry lease. It only provides for the manner in which the application for grant of a quarrying lease shall be dealt with. The Rules do not provide for the grant and renewal of such leases. The rules do not prescribe any particular procedure for granting or renew ing a quarry licence. The State has no power to impose a condition of the grant. The grant of the lease is subject to certain conditions. The conditions imposed by the State are not in the nature of a fee but merely a condition attached to the lease. The terms of the contract are not relevant to the issue involved. The question whether the State can impose a restriction on the right of the petitioners to carry on their business is a matter which must be left to the discretion of the State. [ 410 F H; 411 A B ] 3. The object of the legislation is to regulate the grant, mining rights and the regulation of mines and mineral development. The expression " mining lease " is defined in section 2 (h) of The Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957. Section 2 (i) defines'minor minerals '. Section 2 defines'Minor minerals'as meaning all minerals except those specified in Schedule I. Section 14 of the said Act deals with the grant / renewal of prospecting licences and mining leases in respect thereof. Section 15 of that Act empowers the State Governments to make Rules for regulating grant of mining leases, and the same reads thus: " 15. (1) Every person who is entitled to obtain a mining permit shall apply to the Collector of the district in which he intends to carry out the purposes of this Act. (2). Every application for a mining licence or a quarry permit shall be made to the State Mining Officer of the area in which it is situated. (3) Every application under sub section (1), shall be accompanied by a fee of Rs. 50. (4) Every applicant shall pay a sum of Rs, 500 as the fee payable under sub sections (1)( b) and (c) of section 15. Provided that where the applicant is a company, the application shall be supported by an affidavit sworn by the Managing Director of the company. (5) Every such application shall state the grounds on which the applicant relies. (6) Where the application is made by a company or any member of the association of persons, the applicant shall file with the application a certified copy of the memorandum and the draft of the proposed application together with the documents referred to in sub section. (7) The applicant shall also furnish a copy of his application together, if any, to the District Magistrate concerned. (8) The District Magistrate may, after giving the applicant a reasonable opportunity of being heard, reject the application. (9) The decision of the District Collector shall be final.

The appellant was appointed as a trustee of the temple in the year 1954. He was elected to the office of the trustee and he was elected as a Trustee by the members of his family. In the year 1955, the appellant filed an application for appointment of trustees hip of the respondent's temple under section 6 (9) of the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951. The Deputy Commissioner held that the appellant was not hereditary trustee within the meaning of section 6 of the Act. The High Court dismissed the petition. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the expression " hereditary trustee " in section 6 would include only those persons who were entitled to succeed to the property of the deceased and that the word " succession " in relation to the appellant's father's estate must be construed along with the words " succession to the estate ". HELD: The word " inheritance " in the context of section 2 (1)( b) of Act 19 of 1951 is wide enough to include even such cases. But the definition of " hereditary trustees " in Section 6 (8) of Madras Act, is identical to the definition given in section 2 of the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious & Charitable Endowments (Amendment) Act, 1958.

The deceased was a young man of about 20 years. He had been murdered by the accused and his brother in law, who was sleeping on the western side of the house. On the date of occurrence he was sleeping with his mother in the courtyard. His father was sleeping at that time. When he went to sleep, he saw two persons running ahead of him. He was also sleeping on a bench outside his house. He heard the sh outs of his sister's husband and when he came out of the room he saw the accused standing near the door of the deceased. He ran towards the place where he was sitting. He saw the deceased lying down on the eastern side of his house and the accused was trying to escape from the scene of occurrence. He then rushed to the police station and lodged the FIR. The police registered a case against the accused under section 302 I. P. C. and after investigation submitted charge sheet against the appellant for an offence punishable under section 120B read with section 34 I. PC. The Sessions Judge convicted the appellant under section 120 B I. C., and sentenced him to death. In appeal the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of the appellant but reduced the sentence to imprisonment for life. Allow ing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court has not considered the evidence of PW 4 as it is very clear that the deceased was only mentioning the name of accused Karun akar an as his assailant, this earlier version appears to be corroborated by the contents of the FIR, which was not even suggested by the prosecution. [ 710 E ] 2. It is difficult to accept that the testimony of PW 3 is to be believed because the witness may not have seen the other accused coming together. It would be impossible to believe that the accused will not ask PW 4 to go to the place of occurrence or to give evidence. If the statement of PW 1 is to the effect that the dead body was found at No. 1 in the site plan, there is no reason why the court should be circumspe ct and closely scrutin ise the evidence to come to an un hes it ating conclusion that he is absolutely reliable. [ 711 H; 712 A B ] 3. The trial court erred in convicting the accused solely relying upon the testimony in the first information report. The judgment of the High court is set aside.

The assessee was a Hindu undivided family. It had been carrying on business in the name and style of M / s. Amar chand and Sons, Bombay. In respect of the assessment years 1950 51 to 1954 55, the Income tax Officer sought to assess the income of the deceased for the assessment year 1950 51 under section 34 (1) (b) read with section 24 B of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the income received by the heirs and legal representatives of the late Amar chand was assessable to income tax in the hands of the assessee. On appeal the Appellate Tribunal held that it was not possible to hold that the amount which was received by him as his heir and legal representative was liable to be taxed in the assessment of the income from the estate of the last mentioned person. The High Court also held that since the amounts were received by his heirs and the legal representatives after their death they were liable to tax under section 24 A of the Act. Held, that the words " if he had not died " in section 24 C (2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1961, must be given its natural meaning and the word " or " occurring in section 23 (4) of that Act should be construed accordingly. The expression " any person " in the context means a person who is entitled to receive the income or profits of the previous year. The words " such person " are wide enough to include persons who have no right to receive income or to be treated as an assessee for the purpose of assessment in regard to those years. The word " person " has not been defined in the Act but has been used in the sense of a person having a right to be assessed in respect of income or property. The term " person ", therefore, includes a jur istic person and there can be no doubt that the word'person'in section 2 (22) of Act, 1944, means a " person who has a right or interest in the property ". The word'individual'is generally used in a wide sense and includes a person whose personal rights are affected by reason of his being a member of the joint family. The definition of " person'as given in section 3 (11) of Income tax act, 1922, does not extend to cases where the income is received by a person in the capacity of a coparcen er. The Explanation to section 24 D of the said Act makes it clear that the person who holds the property in the status of a Hindu Undivided Family shall be deemed to be a person liable to pay income tax.

The petitioners were appointed as Assistant Engineers in the Andhra Pradesh State. They were working in various offices of the Andhra State and were posted at Hyderabad, Hyderabad, Secunderabad, Hyderabad and Secunderabad. In the year 1958 they were transferred to Hyderabad by the Government of Andhra Pradesh. The petitioners challenged the validity of section 3 of the Act on the ground that it was violative of article 16 (1) of the Constitution. The High Court held that section 3 was ultra vires the Constitution because it did not impose any restriction on the right of the petitioners to be considered for appointment to a post within the State or Union territory. On appeal by special leave, HELD: (i) Section 3 of The Public Employment (Require ment as to Res idence) Act, 1957 is constitutionally valid. [ 120 B ] (ii) The power conferred upon Parliament under Article 35 (b) of Constitution is subject to the provisions of article 372 of the constitution. It is not necessary to express any opinion whether delegation to the Central and / or State Governments to provide by rules for the further implementing of the law made by Parliament is permissible. [ 121 C D ] (iii) The words'any requirement'cannot be read to warrant something which could have been said more specifically. The word'any'has to be construed in its wid est amplitude so as to include all other requirements of the relevant part of the statute. [ 122 F G ] (iv) The expression " any requirement " in section 3 means only that, if the context requires otherwise, then the expression'any provision'must mean anything which would have the effect of making the provision applicable to the particular case. [ 123 E ] (v) The definition of'residence'in section 2 (e) of The General Clauses Act, 1897, does not exclude the application of the rule of construction to the present case. The words " any condition " in the definition clause are wide enough to include the requirement of residence in a particular part of a State.

The appellant was a post man in the Government of India. He was tried for offences under section 52 of the Indian Post Office Act, 1898 and was convicted by the trial court but acquitted on appeal. The High Court held that the appellant had secre ted the articles which were found in his possession and that he had not been in possession of the articles. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the prosecution had failed to prove that the articles were in the exclusive possession of him and that the presumption could be rebutted if the appellant was able to establish that the article was in his exclusive possession. Held: (i) The appellant had no opportunity to get at the articles seized from the house in question. It was not possible to infer that he was in possession or that he must have been in actual possession of those articles. If the appellant did not possess any such articles he would not be entitled to the benefit of section 52 Of the Indian Postal Act. (ii) The evidence showed that the al mir ah was in the possession of one of the persons who had kept the articles in his custody. The appellant could not therefore be said to have committed theft unless he had been in the custody of the person who had stolen them.

The appellant, a member of the Panchayat, was convicted by the Sessions Judge under section 5 (1)( d) read with section 3 (2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. He was sentenced to imprisonment for two years and a fine of Rs. 500 / and in default to undergo simple imprisonment for one month. In appeal before the High Court, it was contended that the order of the High court was not justified as there was no evidence on record to show that the appellant had knowledge of the order. Dismis sing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High Court should have appreciated the facts and circumstances of the case. [ 118 B ] The High Courts are not bound to interfere with the orders of the courts below unless there is un impeach able evidence that the judicial officer has knowledge of an order which he has made.

The appellant was convicted of the offence under section 302, I. P. C., and sentenced to death by the Sessions Judge. On appeal by special leave, the High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence from life imprisonment to rigorous imprisonment for life. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the evidence of Uj agar Singh was not reliable because he had no enmity with the appellant's brother and that his evidence was unreliable. Held: (i) The evidence of the prosecution witnesses who were interested in the appellant was not sufficient to establish that the appellant had murdered Sheo Sahai. The evidence showed that the deceased was a party to the conspiracy and that he had been falsely implicated. The fact that the accused had a motive to murder Sheo Sahai could not be said to be an incriminating circumstance against him. The appellant had made a confession before the Police Officer which was inadmissible in evidence as it was not admissible in evidence. (ii) The extra judicial confession of the accused to Uj agar singh was not voluntary nor true. It was not proved that the person who had committed the murder of Sheo Sahai was present at the time when the appellant made the confession. (iii) The confession of Uj wara Singh was also not corroborated by any other evidence.

The petitioners, who were the respondents in the writ petition before the High Court, filed a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the electoral roll published on November 16, 1978. They also challenged the validity and correctness of the election to the State Legislative Assembly as well as the validity thereof. The High Court dismissed their petition holding that the petitioners had no locus standi to file the writ petitions. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellants: (1) that the provisions of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, which are mandatory, have not been complied with; (2) that there is no compliance with the provisions contained in section 36 A of the Act; (3) that since the period of 20 days has expired, the declaration of results of the elections should be declared invalid and the result of the poll should be set aside; and (4) that even if the petitioners'names were included in the electoral rolls, they could not be allowed to contest the election because the number of persons whose names were not included in such electoral roll did not exceed the prescribed limit. Dismis sing the appeals, HELD: (i) The power of the High court under Article 227 of the constitution to issue an appropriate writ is discretionary and if the High Courts find that there was not satisfactory explanation far the inordinate delay, it may reject the petition if it finds that the issue of Writ will lead to public inconvenience and interference with rights of others. [ 10 31 C ] (ii) The High Courts have held that the power of this Court under Article 32 of the Constitu tion cannot be exercised arbitrarily or capric iously. It is not possible to accept the contention that the writ petitioner had raised any objection with regard to the date within which the claims and objections could be preferred. [ 11 33 B ] (iii) The question whether in a given case the delay involved is such that it dis's enti ents a person to relief under Article 136 of the Constit uti o n would depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. If the High Cou rt found that there were no sufficient reasons for condoning the delay, the High Cour t would have refused to entertain the petition. But the High C ourt was right in holding that there must be some reasonable ground for the delay.

The appellant company was a public limited company and its directors were prosecuted for the offence of having committed an offence under section 135 (1) of the Companies Act, 1913. The appellant contended that the provisions of section 134 (4) of that Act were not applicable to the case as it did not make any provision in the Act which would be attracted to the facts of the case. Held, that the expression " shall be laid before the general body meeting " in section 132 (2) of this Act means the general meeting of the company or the general meetings of the shareholders thereof. It is clear from the language of the section that the words " shall have been laid before each general body " are wide enough to include the power to give notice of the general assembly and to call a general meeting. The word " shall " in the context means " may ". The word'shall'has been used in section 133 (3) of Act. Section 134 (1)( b) provides that when a general body is dissolved, the members of the board shall cease to hold office. The proviso to section 134 makes it obligatory on the members to send a copy of the balance sheet and profit and loss account to the Registrar within three months after the date of the order of dissolution. The words " may also be sent " in sub section (2), are wide and comprehensive enough to cover the entire period of time prescribed by the section. The legislature had made the provision in section 134 of the Act applicable to cases where the general bodies had been constituted. In the present case, the appellant company had not filed the list of the members but only the members who were required to file the list. The question whether the appellant could be said to have been guilty of offences under sections 76 and 133 (1).

The appellant was convicted under section 5 (1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1950 and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for a period of six months. He filed an appeal in the High Court against his conviction and sentence. The High Court dismissed the appeal but reduced the sentence to one year's rigorous imprisonment. In appeal by special leave it was contended that the provisions of article 14 were not applicable to the case as there was no evidence to show that the appellant had committed any offence or that he was guilty of any other offence. Held: (i) that the words " reasonable classification " in section 5 of the Act must be given their natural meaning and they must be construed in a sense which the common man would have done if he had been charged with offences and criminal acts of a particular kind. (ii) that even though the object of the legislation is not clear, the courts should adopt a liberal approach and give effect to the intention of the legislature. The word " reasonable " has been used in the context of the statute in question and it cannot be said that the legislature intended to confer arbitrary powers on the executive government to direct the court to take into consideration matters which are irrelevant to the purpose of the enactment. (iii) that where the language of the provision is plain and unambiguous, the court may examine its true import and effect and decide whether the statute is such that it is reasonably capable of being interpreted in a way which will make it un workable.

The appellant was appointed as a Professor in the Central Health Service on May 7, 1963. He was promoted to the post of Professor of Radi ology in the pay scale of Rs. 27 50 / and he was posted at the time of his appointment. In the year 1966, the appellant was promoted as an Associate Professor of the Department of Medicine in the Medical College, Delhi. On April 1, 1967, the Government of India issued a notification under r. 8 (2A) of the Central Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1965, which provided that no person who had been appointed as such shall be eligible for appointment to the said post unless he has held a post in the senior grade or post in a substantive capacity. The appellant challenged the validity of the aforesaid notification by filing a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant having not acquired the status of an Assistant Professor in a teaching hospital, he could not claim seniority or eligibility for promotion merely by virtue of these rules. Allow ing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression " in the absence of a candidate'occurring in r. 2 (2A), means " in relation to a person who is already in service of the Union or State ". [ 80 G ] 2. The word " as " in this rule means " as is defined in clause (b) of sub section (2) of section 2 of the Act. It does not mean " in any manner " but only includes " in connection with the affairs of the State." [ 81 B C ] 3. The words " in accordance with the provisions of the rules " in cl. (c) must be read in the context of the proviso to r. 4 (2A). If the appellant is not entitled to hold the post in question, he cannot be considered to have been appointed to the posts of Professor in Maul ana Azad Medical College. [ 82 D E ] 4. The contention that the post was not a teaching post in one discipline is without substance. The mere fact that the petitioner was not drawing a teaching allowance of Rs 200 / p. m. would not entitle him to claim seniority and the appellant being a person possessing the requisite qualification, the respondent was entitled to be considered for appointment as Associate Professor. [ 83 F H; 84 A ] 5. The second respondent was not entitled for the benefit of the first proviso to Rule 8 (2)( ii) of Part I of the First Schedule to the Indian Medical Council Act, 1956.

The workmen of the Company, who were employed in the Company and were working as such, had been paid bonus at the rate of Rs. 9 per month for the period from April 1, 1961 to March 31, 1963. In the year 1962 63, the Company was paying a minimum wage of Rs 100 per month. On the basis of the total wages received by the workmen, the Tribunal held that there was no justification for fixing the minimum wage at Rs. 73 per month on the basis that the workmen were entitled to the same scale of pay as the permanent workmen. The Tribunal also found that the Company had not produced any evidence to show that the minimum wages fixed by the Tribunal were higher than what it was getting in the previous years. It further held that the Tribunal was wrong in holding that the dearness allowance should be fixed at Rs 75 per month instead of Rs 75. This finding was confirmed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The Tribunal committed an error of law in relying upon the decision of this Court in the case of Fr ench Motor Car Co. Ltd. vs Workmen;, [ 1959 ] S. C. R. 925, followed. (ii) The claim for higher bonus could not have been based on the availability of surplus according to the Full Bench Form ula. The award of the Tribunal is set aside. [ 677 E F ] (iii) The question whether the bonus payable to the workmen under the Award can be fixed only after taking into account the consolidated wages which are being paid by the Company to its employees cannot be decided by the Industrial Tribunal. [ 678 B D ] (iv) The contention that the bonus in respect of the workmen in the present case was not based on any particular wage but on the ground that certain clerical staff was being paid less than 90 % of the minimum basic wages, is without substance. [ 679 G H ] (v) The demand for higher wage was made on the strength of the existing wage structure and the Tribunal has rightly taken into account all the relevant factors including the wage scales prevailing in the company.

The appellant, a partnership firm, was assessed to tax for the assessment year 1960 61. In the assessment proceedings for the years 1960 61 and 1961 62, the Income tax Officer had no reason to believe that by reason of the omission or failure on the part of the assessee to make a return under section 139 for any assessment year, income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment for that year. The Commissioner, in exercise of his powers under section 148 of the Act, issued notice under section 147 of the Income Tax Act, 1961. The appellant filed an appeal before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner against the order of the Commissioner. The Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal holding that the notice under Section 148 was invalid because it did not comply with the requirements of section 151 (2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The High Court held that the Income - tax Officer could not have issued a notice under sections 148 and 149 of the I. T. Act, as there was no compliance with the requirement of section 150 (2). Dismis sing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Income tax officer had no material before him which could satisfy the requirements under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. [ 447 G ] 2. The fact that the appellant's statement was recorded under section 161 of the Criminal Procedure Code is not sufficient to hold that he was satisfied that this was a fit case for the issue of a notice Under section 148. [ 448 B C ] 3. The facts found by the Income taxation Officer were not correct. The report submitted by him was not relevant to the assessment for the accounting year in question. [ 449 E F ] 4. The provisions of section 148 are clear enough to show that the Commissioner was satisfied about the existence of the reasons for issuing a notice. [ 450 D ] 5. The expression " reason to suspect that the income chargeable under section 149 has escaped assessments for that particular year " does not mean that the Assessing Officer must give reasons for coming to the conclusion that the explanation given by the assessee is not satisfactory. [ 452 H ] 6. The word " reason " used in section 148 is not mandatory but only directory. It is not necessary that the reasons should be given for the purpose of giving the notice. The words " reason for such belief " do not mean " reason ".

The appellant, a partnership firm, was assessed to tax under the Indian Income tax Act of 19 18. In the assessment year 1948 49, the appellant claimed relief under section 25 (4) of the Indian income tax Act, 1922 on the ground that it had transferred its business in the name and style of " M / s. Gan non Dun ker ley & Co." and that the said business was not liable to be taxed under the Act of 1922 as it did not have any income from the business carried on by it. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim for relief under Section 25 (2) of that Act. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the appellant was not entitled to relief under the section because the business was carried on at the time when the assessee was carrying on his business and that he was not a mere change in the constitution of the partnership. He also held that there was no succession to the business and therefore the question of relief under sections 25 (1) and 26 (2), could not arise. The High Court dismissed the appeals. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The appellant's case is covered by section 25 of the Act. [ 95 C ] (ii) The business which was carried out by the appellant in the hands of the partners was not an asset or business but only a number of branches. It was not necessary that the business should have been carried on in the names of the persons who were partners. [ 96 G H; 97 A B ] (iii) The fact that the partnership was dissolved in the year 1939 cannot affect the question whether the business continued in existence after the death of the partner. If the business had been carried out at the date of dissolution, then the same would be governed by the provisions of section 25. [ 97 F G ] (iv) The word " business " has not been defined in the Act and the definition of the expression " business ", in section 25, means any business carried out in India and includes a business carried in any form of commerce or manufacture or any adv enture or concern in the nature of trade or commerce. [ 98 E F ] (v) The words " business carried or carried on " in section 2 (5) are wide enough to cover the present case. The business of the appellant being carried on within the meaning of section 2, the business must be deemed to have been trans acted at the relevant time.

The appellant, a Hindu widow of the deceased, was the sole heir of her husband. She died in 1960 leaving behind her two sons and three daughters. On his death she became entitled to a share in the joint family property. The appellant's father had executed a will on March 31, 1955 beque ath ing his properties to him. In the Will he made an application for partition of the suit properties which were allotted to him by the Joint Civil Judge, Senior Division, Sangli. The trial court held that the appellant was entitled to 1 / 4th share in all the properties. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the appellant could not be treated as a separate coparcen er; (ii) the suit was barred by limitation under section 6 of the Act; and (iii) the respondent had no right to claim partition. Dismis sing the appeal, HELD: (i). The appellant was not entitled to any share in his own property. [ 770 B ] (ii). The question whether the appellant is entitled to the share in respect of the joint Hindu family property has been decided by the Bombay High Court in Rang ubai Lal ji vs Laxman Lal ji, A. I. R. 1974 Bom. L. R., referred to. (iii). The decision of the Bombay Court in Sank u vs Narayan rao Gopal rao Patil, A I. C. R, followed. (iv) The appellant being a coparcen er, was entitled only to one half share in each of the properties and not to the other half. [ 771 F G ] (v) The High Courts have taken a contrary view. It is true that the law requires that the interest of a Hindu Mit aksh ara coparcen er should be deemed to be the share of the heirs but the fact remains that the shares are not so divided. The position is different when the share is given to a coparcen ary property. If the share or the share does not belong to the coparcen ary, then the share becomes a part of the estate of the coparcen er. [ 772 E H ] (vi) The principle that the coparcen ers must be regarded as having got their share in a joint family cannot be ignored merely because they may have received a share from the joint property. But if the coparcen ery is carried out by the members of the family, the share would be a part and parcel of the property. This principle applies equally to the case where the share has been acquired by the coparcen al coparcen er and the share devol ves upon the surviving members of a coparcen ery.

The appellant Corporation was established in the year 1956 under the, and it was governed by the provisions of the. The respondent Corporation was a statutory body constituted under the Act. Under section 11 (2) of the Act, the Central Government had power to make rules for carrying out the purposes of the said Act. Section 11 (1) provided that every employer shall be bound to comply with such rules as may be made by the Central Govern ment from time to time. The employees of the Corporation were not entitled to any pension or gratuity. The Corporation was also empowered to frame regulations for regulating the conditions of service of its employees. In exercise of the powers conferred by section 11 of the, the Corporation framed Regulations which were published on January 19, 1956. Regulation 19 (2), which was amended in 1976, provided that the Corporation would have no right to retire any employee who has completed 20 years of service. The appellant corporation challenged the validity of the regulation before the High Court contending that the Regulation was violative of Article 14 and 16 of the Constitution. It was contended that the Regulations were ultra vires Articles 14 and 21 of the Con sti t ution and that they were arbitrary and unreasonable. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the regulations were ultra vi o l ative and were not enforceable. Allow ing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Regulations are valid and constitutional. [ 221 G ] 2. The Regulation is an integral part of the scheme of the Indian Electricity Act, 1910. The regulations are framed for the purpose of securing uniformity among the employees of various categories of the employees in the Corporation. They are intended to be implemented by the Corporation and the Central Govt. in consultation with the State Governments. The Central Government is competent to modify the scales of remuneration and other terms and conditions of services applicable to all employees of a Corporation. [ 222 D E ] 3. The expression " employ ees " in the definition clause includes within its ambit persons employed in connection with the affairs of the Union or of a State. The word'employ'in the context means'engaged in'or'in connection'with the work of a particular kind or category of employment. The term'employ ee'in this sense means a person whose services are rendered by one department to another. The words'employ ees'and'workmen'in section 2 (i) of that Act are used in the same sense in which they are understood in common parlance. [ 223 F G ] 4. The definition of'employee'in s. 2 (e) of, the Act is wide enough to include persons employed by the State Government in connection therewith. The meaning of the word'employee ', therefore, must be given effect to. [ 224 B C ] 5. The Board of Directors of the Company is a statutory authority created under the provisions Of the Act and the Rules framed thereunder. The functions of the Board are entrusted to the Executive. The Executive Committee is vested with the power to regulate the conditions and the duties of the staff. The power to fix the age of retirement is conferred upon the Executive Committee. The Standing Committee of the Central Board of Trustees is appointed by the President. The Chairman of the Governing Body is the Chairman of that Committee. He is the Secretary of the Executive Council. The Chief Executive Officer of the Life Insurance Corporation is the appointing authority. The General Manager of the LIC is the Managing Director of the company. The Managing Director is the Appointing Authority. The Regional Director of a company is the controlling authority. Therefore, the General Manager is the Controlling Authority. [ 225 H;

The appellants were convicted under section 120 (b) of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for a period of two years. They filed an appeal before the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal, it was contended that the letter did not constitute contempt of court as there was no intention on their part to sc andal ise the Hon'ble Judge or to lower him in the administration of justice. Allow ing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The letter does not constitute any contempt of Court. It is necessary to state here that if the public debate is addressed to the Chief Justice, he will be more careful in dealing with matters concerning the administration and the public. [ 247 B ] 2. The letters written by the appellants were correct. The contents of the letter are true and correct. There is nothing to show that the appellants committed any contempt. The High Court proceeded on the basis that the letters written were wrong. The appellants had no case that they committed any Contempt of Court, but the High court proceeded on a wrong assumption that the alleged contempt was committed by the appellant. [ 248 F G ] 3. The judgment is clearly unsustainable. The order of the High Cour t cannot be sustained. [ 249 E ] 4. The question whether the Judges were guilty of contempt of the Court has to be decided on facts whether the Judge concerned did speak on the matter attributed to him. If the speech of any Judge is critic ised and if it becomes a disputed question of fact as to whether any Judge did speak or not as is alleged by the writer the matter would have to be ascertained by the court on facts. [ 250 C D ] 5. The Supreme Court should have dropped the proceeding. [ 251 H;

The petitioner was a company registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. It was carrying on business of manufacturing and selling goods in India. In the course of its business it had entered into an agreement with the Government of India for the purpose of carrying out certain activities which were to be carried out by the petitioner as a result of which the petitioner company was incorporated. The petitioner company had been assessed to income tax for the assessment years 1948 56 and 1949 60 and the Income Tax Officer issued notices to the petitioner under section 5 (1) of the Act calling upon him to show cause why he should not be assessed to tax. The assessee filed his objections against the proposed levy of tax but the same were rejected. On appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the provisions of sections 6 and 7 of the Indian Income tax Act were ultra vires and void and directed the petitioner to pay the tax. He also imposed a penalty of Rs. 2 lakhs on the petitioner. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the impugned Act was violative of article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as it did not make any provision for the imposition of penalty or for the recovery of tax. HELD: (i) The power conferred by section 5 is wide enough to include within its ambit all matters relating to taxation. [ 460 F ] (ii) The powers possessed by the Central Government under section 3 are very wide and can be exercised only when the circumstances mentioned therein justify such a delegation. The power to impose penalty is not confined to any particular class of cases but extends to all cases where the penalty has been levied or imposed. The word " substantial " in section 5 means something more than mere inaction or failure. The expression " substantial injustice " is not limited to a maximum period of eight years. The words " substantial justice " cannot be construed to mean " adequate relief ". The expression'substantial injustice'is not defined in the Act. The meaning given to the word " sufficient " in the context of the statute is " substantial ", " substantial ". The word'substantial'is generally understood to mean substantial injustice. The court must look at the facts and circumstances of each case and decide whether the conduct of the person charged is such as would bring the case within the mischief of the law. [ 461 C D;

The appellant, a company registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was carrying on business of selling and dealing in various commodities. It had its office at Delhi. The appellant's case was that it was not an " establishment " as defined in section 2 (5) of the Act. The High Court held that the activity of the Federation was a " trade or business " within the meaning of section 2. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The definition of " commercial establishment " given in section (2) of section 1 of the is wide enough to include any place where the business is carried on by a person who is engaged in the production or manufacture of goods for sale or for other purposes. [ 354 E ] (2)( a) The expression " commercial establishments " has been used in the definition of the word " commercial " in section 11 of the English Act which means " any premises including any place wherein any trade, business, profession or v ocation is carried out ". The expression'commercial establishment'is wide and includes any place in which any trade or profession is carried or carried on. The expression is wide in its amplitude and includes every place where a trade, profession, trade or occupation is carried upon. The words " any trade " are of wide import and must be construed in their wid est sense. [ 355 G H; 356 A B ] (b) The activities of the appellant were not merely incidental to the main purpose of the society but were also incidental to its primary object. The activities carried on in the premises were not incidental or ancillary to the primary purpose of a trade or trade. The activity of a registered society, therefore, could not be said to be a " commercial activity " within section 2 of the. [ 356 C D ] (c) The activity carried on was not a " business " because by the Memorandum of Association, the appellant was not entitled to carry on the business of the Society.

The appellant was a Hindu undivided family consisting of his father, the respondent and his two sons. The income tax officer held that the amount received by the appellant as an allowance for the purpose of ann uity was revenue expenditure and not taxable under section 4 (3)( viii) of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the assessing authority. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the payment of pension was in the nature of a capital receipt and not a payment in money. Held: (1) that the sum of Rs. 36, 396 / which was paid as an annual rent of the assessee's predecessor in interest was not agricultural income within the meaning of section 4 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1961. (2) that there was no evidence to show that the appellant had any right to receive or recover the amount of the pension from the respondent. (3) that even if the amount was a capital payment, the amount could be taxed only if it was an ann uity. (4) that in the absence of any material to show the nature and character of the payment, it was not taxable.

The appellants in Civil Appeal No. 441 of 1981 were appointed as Supervisors'A'and they were promoted to the post of Chargeman II on completion of 2 years'satisfactory service. They filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order dated 2nd February, 1981 passed by the State Government under which their pay scales were revised from time to time. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the appellants had been given the same scale of pay as was granted to them in the case of Supervisors'B'and that the respondents could not be allowed to draw the same pay scale as those who were regularly appointed as Supervisor'A '. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the appellants having been given promotion as Chargeman Grade I w. e. f. 1. 4. 1983 and (ii) the respondents having been promoted as Chargeman II w. ef. 1 / 3 / 79, they should have been given all the benefits of the higher pay scale. Dismis sing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. 1 The appellants are entitled to get the benefit of the judgment of this Court dated 2 nd February, 1982 rendered in Civil Appeals Nos. 441 and 442 of 1981. [ 10 42 C ] 1. 2 The appellants of these two appeals are also entitled to the same relief as was given to the appellants in the other two cases. [ 11 43 E ] 1: 2. The appellants have been denied the same benefit as was extended to the respondents in the said appeals. [ 12 43 F ] 1 (a) The appellants were given the benefit as per the directions of this court dated 2. 2. 1981. The respondents were given promotion to the posts of Chargeman I w l. e., the appellants were promoted as Foreman Grade II w l th t the posts in the cadre of Chargeman III. The promotions were made on the basis of seniority cum merit. The respondent no. 1 was given the higher grade of Rs. 1200 /- as he was found fit for promotion to Chargeman II. The promotion was made on completion o f 2 years of service. The promotional avenues were given to him as Chargeman I and the appellants. The grievance of the petitioners is that though they were given a higher pay than the respondents, they were not given the difference of back wages and promotion to higher posts. [ 13 G H; 14 A B ] 1.( b) The respondents have not been given any opportunity to show cause why they should not be given the said pay scale and the promotion to lower posts. The only effect of the decision of this Tribunal is that the persons who were given such promotion as Supervisors Grade I and who were subsequently promoted as Charg em an ts, would be entitled to be treated as Chargeman Gr. II. [ 15 D E ] 2. 1 It is true that the promotion of the respondents to the higher posts was made after due consideration of the matter by the authorities concerned but the fact remains that the said promotion was not given to them. Therefore, the respondents cannot be deprived of the same. [ 16 E F ] 2.( a) There is no provision in the Rules for giving the benefit to the persons like the respondents. [ 17 G ] 2 (b) If there is a conflict between the rules and the provisions of the Act, the rules will prevail.

The appellant, a private operator of the State Transport Undertaking, was granted a permit by the Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation for plying buses on the route to be given to him. He applied for grant of permits in respect of the said routes and also applied for renewal of his permit. The Regional Transport Authority rejected the application of the appellant on the ground that he had not been given an opportunity of being heard before the grant of the permits. The appellant filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the grant. The High Court held that the appellant's application for grant was barred by section 63 (7) of the Act as it did not comply with the requirements of section 63. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The expression " any person " in section 2 (29 A) means a person who is holding a valid licence or a contract carriage permit under which he has been authorised to ply a transport vehicle. [ 10 B ] (2) The words " any other person " occurring in section 5 (1)( d) are wide enough to include persons who have no experience in the transport business. It is difficult to understand why the legislature intended that the word " such " should be read as " any one who is not a person " within the meaning of section 2. [ 11 C D ] (3) The proviso to section 63 does not say that the rules of preference will apply only if there is a change in the policy of the Government. The rule is a rule of preference and not a rule. [ 12 G H; 13 A ] (4) The object of the proviso to Section 63 (1), is to give preference to persons having more than two years'experience in a transport service. The proviso makes it clear that the rule is applicable only when the applicant is a person whose application for a stage carriage permit is made after the specified date. The scheme does not make any distinction between the two categories of persons. The first category is covered by the proviso. The second category is not covered by clause (iv). The third category is excluded from consideration because the rule provides that the concession shall be given only if the person concerned has worked in the motor vehicle for a period of at least five years. The provision is therefore discriminatory and violative of article 14 of the Constitution.

The respondent was the sole proprietor of a business carried on by one of its partners. He had been assessed to sales tax in respect of his turnover for the years 1948 49 and 1949 50, but he did not pay the tax due from him as required under section 19 (2)( c) of the Act. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the respondent was liable to pay sales tax on the turnover of the transferor and directed the appellant to pay the amount of sales tax payable by him. In appeal, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the State Government could not be made liable to payment of sales Tax on the sale of goods effected by the transferee, because the liability to pay Sales Tax arose only when the transfer took place. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the order of the State government was illegal and ultra vires. The fact that the registered instrument was executed by the respondent is not conclusive. It is true that the word " assessment " in the scheme of the sales tax and income tax legislation is a term of wide import. The word'assessment'in the context of the Income tax Act means assessment or re computation of the tax. But the word'assess'in section 19 of the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939, which is a part of the same statute, has no application to the present case.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk in the respondent's department. He was suspended from service on account of his misconduct and he was dismissed from service by an order dated February 2, 1955. On appeal to the High Court, it was contended that the order of dismissal was illegal because the appellant had not been given reasonable opportunity of being heard before passing the order. Held: (1) that the appellant was entitled to be reinstated with full backwages for the period during which he was actually in office. (2) that section 61 of the Bombay Re organisation Act, 1960, did not apply to the case of arrears of salary. (3) that there was no duty cast upon the Government servant to pay salary if he was in receipt of any money or other property. (4) that under section 60 (2)( b) of the Act, the liability of the State to pay salaries is limited only to the amount of wages payable to the employee. (5) that even though the appellant could have paid the amount due to him, he was not entitled to the payment of the salary.

The appellant was the owner of a coal mine in which the respondents were carrying on mining operations. The appellant's father, who was the lessee of the coal mines, had leased out the same to the respondent for a period of 10 years and thereafter he had been paying rent to the appellant. In the year 1941, the appellant filed a suit against the respondents for possession of the said coal. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal. On appeal by special leave, it was contended that the finding of the courts below that the appellant had failed to prove that the respondents had knowledge of the appellant'S possession of his coal mines is erroneous. Held: (i) The burden of proof has not been discharged by the appellant as the appellant did not have any knowledge of its possession. The onus of proving that the respondent had knowledge or information of the fact that the coal was lying in the encroached area lies upon the appellant and not on the respondents. The burden is on the appellant to prove this fact. [ 488 B C ] (ii) The presumption under section 114 of the Evidence Act is rebut table and the onus of proof is on him. It is open to the plaintiff to establish that the defendant had knowledge about the alleged encroachment. But the burden of proving the existence of the facts so proved is on a party who asserts the right, and it is for the defendants to show that they had knowledge that the property was in their possession. [ 489 F G ] (iii) The onus is on an applicant who seeks to prove the existence or non existence of a fact. He must also prove that he had knowledge and that he knew what he was doing. The mere fact that he did not know the exact nature of the land does not mean that he was aware of the existence. The question whether the appellant was entitled to the benefit of the provisions of section 115 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, would depend on the facts and circumstances of each case.

The appellant was a contractor of the respondent company. He was employed as a sub contractor in the appellant's factory and he was charged with misconduct under r. 18 (a) of the Standing Orders, which provided that no such enquiry shall be held unless the employer had given him notice to show cause why his services should not be terminated. The appellant contended that the termination of service was bad because it was made without giving any reason and therefore the order terminating his services was illegal. Held, that the appellant was entitled to reinstatement with full back wages. The question whether the termination was mala fide or was a mere irregularity of an act of victi mis ation or unfair labour practice could not arise at all. The fact that the employer did not give any reasons for terminating the services of the employee would not make the order invalid. The decision of this Court in Par shot am Lal Dhingra vs Union of India, [ 1960 ] 1 S. C. R. 66, referred to.

The appellant, a tenant of a building in the town of Ahmedabad, was granted a lease of a cinema theatre by the respondent for a period of three years. On August 19, 1954, the appellant filed a suit against the respondent and his brother for a declaration that he had no right to exhibit films on the ground that they were not public ations within the meaning of section 2 (1) of the Bombay R ents, Hotel and Lod ging House Rates Control Act, 1947, as amended by the Bombay Rent Act, 1958, and that the respondent had no power to grant a lease or to have acted in contravention of the terms of the agreement dated November 27, 1954. The Trial Court dismissed the suit but the High Court allowed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the expression " case " in section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure means a suit instituted before the commencement of the Act and that since the question whether a party is entitled to lead evidence in support of his claim has been decided by the Trial Court, the order passed by the High court should be set aside. HELD: (i) The word'case'in section 115 of the C. P. C. must be construed as a reference to a suit pending at the time when the suit is filed. [ 442 E ] (ii) The words " case ", in section 2 of the Civil Procedure Code, are wide enough to include a suit which is not merely a suit or proceeding between the parties to a dispute, but also a suit in which the rights of the parties are likely to be affected. The word " case'is not restricted to the whole of the proceeding only and does not mean any other proceeding except a suit. [ 444 F G ] (iii) The expression " suit " in the context of section 92 is wide enough not to include an application under section 92, but it includes a suit where the plaintiff is sought to be evicted from the premises. The expression'case ', in section 91 of the Evidence Act, means a civil proceeding and is not confined to the proceedings relating to a contract. It is not limited to the entire proceeding but extends to the trial of a suit and to all proceedings arising therefrom. [ 445 B D ] (iv) Section 92 of C. Ps. is a special provision dealing with the subject matter of a proceeding. The provisions of section 93 of the Indian Evidence Act do not apply to a proceeding instituted before a Court subordinate to such High Court. The words'case " are wide in their import to the entirety of the matter in issue. [ 446 H;

The respondent was appointed as a temporary employee in the appellant Corporation. He was appointed on contract basis for a fixed term of one year and he continued to be in service till 30th August, 1985. On his appointment, he was given an extension of his period of probation upto 30th of August, 1986 by an order dated 1st June, 1983. In the meanwhile, the respondent was allowed to continue in service beyond 30th of July, 1985 but he was not granted any further extension. The respondent filed a Writ Petition before the High Court challenging the order of termination of his services. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the respondent had put forward at the time of his initial appointment and that he could not claim salary up to the date of his appointment. Allow ing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The order passed on review is wholly unsustainable. [ 245 F ] 2. The Division Bench of the High court has rightly set aside the order dated 24. 3. 1988. [ 246 E ] 3. The judgment of the Division Bench dated 24 / 3. 88 does not make out that the Respondent was entitled to be treated as a regular employee who had a vested right to continue to hold the post until he attained 58 years of age. The true position that emerges from the material on record is that the respondents were entitled to the salary upto the date when they were appointed and no orders of extension of service were passed on them. [ 247 B C ] 4. The fact that the interim order which had been passed on 10. 7. 86 did not make it clear that the order was not in the nature of a contract and the subsequent orders extending his period upto 30th August 1985 cannot be said to be a direction to extend the period of his service beyond 30 days. [ 248 G H; 249 A ] 5. The question whether the respondent should be treated to be an invalid one or not is a matter of policy. It is not necessary to set out all the facts and circumstances of the case.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 I. P. C. and sentenced to imprisonment for life. He filed a petition before the High Court of Andhra Pradesh challenging his conviction and sentence. The High Court dismissed the petition on the ground that it was not maintainable because the Sessions Judge had no jurisdiction to entertain the appeal against the order of acquittal, but only on the question whether the view taken by the Sessions judge was correct or not. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High court was justified in interfering with the order passed by the trial court. [ 369 E ] (2) The power of the High court to interfere with an order of the acquittal is very wide and can be exercised only when there are compelling reasons justifying its interference. But where two views of the evidence are possible, one which is more probable than the other, the one which favour's the accused must prevail. [ 370 F G ] (3) The test laid down by the Privy Council in Sheo Swarup vs Em per or, A. I. R. 1971 S. C., 460, applied. (4) The principles laid down in San wat Singh's case are fully applicable to the present case. [ 371 D ] (5) The principle that the accused is entitled to the benefit of any doubt arising from the possibility of a du ality of views, the possible view in favour of the accused should be as nearly reasonably probable as that against him. If two reasonably probable and even ly balanced views of both the circumstances are possible and the reasonable doubt does not arise, the benefit thereof cannot be claimed by the accused. [ 372 B C ] (6) The presumption under section 114 of the Evidence Act is not weak ened by the fact that the prosecution has failed to establish the guilt beyond reasonable doubt. It is not necessary that the burden of proof lies on the accused person to prove the existence of all the circumstances constituting the offence alleged against him, unless the contrary is proved. [ 373 H;

The appellant was a public servant. He was convicted by the Special Judge, CBI for offences under section 5 (1)( d) read with section 5 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years and to pay a fine of Rs. 2, 000 / in default to suffer further rigorous imprisonment. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to one of life imprisonment. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts had no jurisdiction to entertain an appeal against the order of conviction passed by the trial court as there was no provision in the Code of Criminal Procedure which required the Chief Justice of India to hear appeals from the judgment of the High court. Dismis sing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The power conferred upon the High courts under article 124 of the Constitution is not confined to the powers of the Supreme Court or the High, Court under Article 226 of the Constit uti o n. [ 310 E ] 2. The High Court has jurisdiction to try all cases arising out of the discharge of its functions under any law made by Parliament. It is not necessary to examine the question whether the High Cour t can exercise its jurisdiction under article 136 of the constitution when the case is before it. [ 311 F G ] 3. The expression " other than the Chief justice " in clause (e) of sub article (4) of article 124 must be given a wide meaning so as to include within its ambit the High est Court. [ 312 B C ] 4. The word'person'in the context of the Indian Penal Code means a person who is in the service of the Government of India or of a State Government. [ 313 D ] 5. The words'person ', used in the section are not sy non y mous with the word'individual '. They have been used in different's enses and they have been defined in the Indian Evidence Act. The definition of the term'person " in section 2 (e), includes every person who, at the time of the commission of the offence, is a member of the armed forces of the Union. [ 314 A B ] 6. The phrase'person in charge of a police station'is not restricted to the members of the Armed Forces of the country. It may also include persons who are employed in connection with the affairs of the State. But the expression'person found guilty'in section 5 does not mean only those persons who were charged with the aid of section 5. [ 315 H; 316 A ] 7. Section 5 (2) of the Act provides that nothing contained in the Act shall apply to any proceeding relating to the investigation of an offence punishable under the Act. [ 317 B ] 8. The provisions of section 6 (1) of The Prevention of corruption Act, and section 161 of the Code do not make any distinction between the officers and the subordinate judiciary. [ 318 B ] 9.
