The object of the Legislature in enacting the Act is to provide for the appointment of a judge of the high Court and the High. Court. The legislature has not enacted any law regulating the procedure for the conduct of the proceedings of the criminal courts. The Act does not contemplate any such procedure. [ 319 B ] 10. The scheme of the statute shows that the legislature intended to provide a special procedure for dealing with the matters connected with the administration of justice. The general rule is that the Judges should not be called upon to act judicially. The language of the section clearly indicates that the judges should not act as judges of the Court. If the intention of the legislature was to provide that the particular matter should be tried by a Judge of the highest rank, then the legislature would have provided that the same procedure should be followed in the matter of making the appointments.

The appellant was a member of the Saha caste. He had been elected to the West Bengal Legislative Assembly from the said constituency in which he was a candidate for election as a member. In March, 1965, he filed an election petition challenging the validity of the election of the appellant on various grounds. The High Court dismissed his petition holding that the appellant belonged to the Scheduled Caste and not to the scheduled castes. On appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the respondent that the question whether the appellant belongs to a Scheduled Caste or not must be decided in the light of the evidence adduced in the case. Held: (i) The appellant's contention that the respondent's claim to belong to the Schedule Caste is irrelevant because the evidence before the Tribunal did not show that there was within the Sun ri caste group of the Sun r is who bore the sur name Saha. The Tribunal came to its conclusion that the evidence showed that the appe l l ant belonged to a smaller caste group. The finding that the Tribunal had come to the conclusion that there were no other persons belonging to the same caste but those who bore their sur name, cannot be accepted. The fact that the tribunal went wrong in relying upon the evidence in the present case does not alter the natural meaning of the words " excluding them ". It is nobody's case that there is any evidence to show that the appellants belonged to another caste. There is also no evidence to establish that the first respondent belonged to any other caste. The appellant could not therefore be held to belong the Scheduled Castes specified in item 40.

The appellant, a tenant of the flat in question, was the owner of a flat on the second floor of a building called " Ganga Vihar ", which belonged to him. He had been paying rent to the landlord for the use and occupation of his flat. The respondent No. 1, who was the tenant of a Flat in the said building, filed a suit against the appellant for recovery of possession of the said flat. In the written statement filed by the appellant, it was contended that he was not the tenant within the meaning of section 18 (2) of the Bombay R ents, Hotel and Lod ging House Rates Control Act, 1947, as he was only a tenant in respect of the premises. It was further contended that the appellant was liable to be evicted under section 19 (2)( b) of that Act. Held, that the word'relinquishment'used in section 19 of the Act is not a term of art and must be construed in favour of the landlord. The words are " the lessee or any person acting or purporting to act on behalf of the tenant ". The expression " relinquishment " does not mean an assignment of the tenancy but means a relinquishment of the right of the lessor to the tenant. The word " relinquishment'has no meaning in the context of the Transfer of Property Act. The definition of " relinquishment ", in section 18 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, includes a relinquishment. The expression'relinquishment ', therefore, cannot be read in isolation. The distinction between an assignment and relinquishment is well settled. The intention of the legislature in enacting section 18 is to make a contract void able. The section does not speak of relinquishment or giving up of possession. The mere fact that the landlord was a tenant would not make him a lessee. The terms of the section do not say that the tenant dis appeared from the scene altogether. The language employed in section 15 is clear. The phrase " relinquishment of his tenancy " is not defined in the Act. Section 18 (1) of this Act defines " relinquishment ". The word'surrender'is not sy non y mous with'relinquishment '. The word is not used in the section. The meaning of the word " surrender " is very wide. The dictionary meaning of " surrender ", is " to give up " or " to take over ". The meaning given to the word is " surrender ". The words " relinquishment or surrender " are not sy Non y mous. The term " relinquishment is " is used in a statute, which gives a right to the transferor to get back the possession of his interest. A transfer of property is not made in the strict sense of the term. The transfer of the property is a lease. The legal position is that the transferee becomes liable by reason of the transfer of a lease by the tenant in favour. The proviso to section 18 makes it clear that the transfer is not to be treated as a relinquishment if the transfer was made by the landlord in favour or by the wife of the original tenant.

The appellant company was a partnership firm. It had its factory at Bombay and the employees of the respondent company were also paid dearness allowance, but it was not in dispute that the company was paying dearness allowance to its employees. In the year 1974 the company made an application for revision of wage scales on the ground that the Company was not entitled to pay higher than what it was entitled to under the revised pay scales. The Tribunal rejected the application holding that the workmen were entitled to get dearness allowance as per the revised scale. The Industrial Tribunal held that the employer was liable to pay dearness allowance only if there was no change in the rate of dearness allowance or any other factor which could be taken into account by the Tribunal. On appeal by special leave, the Court, HELD: 1. The question whether the Tribunal was right in directing the payment of dearness allowances based on the revised wage scales is a matter of policy. [ 182 B ] 2. The decision of this Court in the case of Workmen of Hindustan Steel Ltd. vs Their Workmen,;, referred to. 3. The award of the Tribunal is set aside and the reference is remanded to the Tribunal for fresh disposal. [ 183 D E ] 4. The appellant has been directed to pay the dearness allowance and other benefits admissible to the employees. The amount of dearness relief should be paid within three months from today.

The appellant, a sugar mill, was awarded an award by the Industrial Tribunal for the period from January 1, 1957 to March 31, 1958. The respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the award on the ground that it was not made in accordance with section 2 (vi) of the Act and that the award was invalid as it did not comply with the provisions of section 15 of the Industrial Disputes Act. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the Labour Court had jurisdiction to entertain the application under section 15 Of the Act before it was amended. The decision of this Court in the South Indian Bank Ltd. vs A. R. Chacko, [ 1964 ] S. C. 15, followed.

The appellant was a Sub Divisional Officer in the Public Works Department, and was charged with misappropriation of certain amounts. He was convicted under section 409, Indian Penal Code, for having committed an offence under section 465, Indian penal Code, and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for one year. On appeal by the State Government, the High Court held that the sanction was necessary as there was no evidence on record to show that the appellant had been guilty of any criminal misappropriation or forgery. Held, that the conviction's and sentences passed against the appellant were illegal. The appellant could not be prosecuted under section 420, Indian. Penal Code because he did not get the money from the treasury, nor was he a public servant who had received it. The prosecution was bad for want of sanction under section 197 (1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The sanction was required under section 196 (1), Cr. P. C., and the appellant could have been tried under section 471, I. P.. C. But the question whether sanction was essential or not must depend on the special circumstances of each case.

The assessee was a public limited company incorporated in the State of Travancore and Cochin. It had its registered office in the former Cochin State, which was then in the United King dom. In the assessment year 1950 51 the assessee claimed deduction of Rs. 79, 275 as loss from its business profits under section 32 (1) of the Indian Income tax Act 1922. The Income Tax Officer disallowed the claim on the ground that the assessee's income was not liable to be included in the total income of the assessee for the purpose of computing the rate of tax. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the banking business of the appellant was one and indi visible and that the profit or gains of the business carried on by it could not be brought into the taxable income of any person. On appeal the Appellate Tribunal held that since the assessee was carrying on business in the Travancore State he was entitled to deduct the losses incurred in the business in Travancore State. The High Court also held that in view of the provisions of section 24 (2) of Travancore Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1949, the assessee could not claim deduction of the losses sustained in Travancore States because the proviso to section 24 of the Travancore Income Tax Act, 1922 did not apply to the case. Held, that the words " business in British India " in section 24 were wide enough to include business in an Indian State and so the proviso was not applicable to the present case. The word " business " in the proviso must mean business in India and therefore the proviso would not apply.

The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1960. It had a factory at Calcutta and it had its factory at Bombay. In July, 1947, the respondent company entered into an agreement with its employees for the purpose of fixing the age of retirement at 60. On August 1, 1948, the Company made certain changes in the conditions of service of its employees. The employees were given the option to retire at the age when they would be governed by the rules applicable to them. The respondent company also agreed that the age should be fixed at 60 but the company did not agree to this proposal. The Tribunal held that the respondent's case was covered by the decision of the Tribunal in the matter of fixation of the age at 60 as regards the pensionable age of superannuation. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The Tribunal has failed to notice that the trend in Bombay region was to fix the retirement age at 55 or at 58. [ 429 F ] (ii) The fact that the Tribunal had found that in some cases the pattern adopted by the company was different from what was decided by the Tribunal is not correct. [ 430 G H; 431 A B ] (iii) The question whether the Tribunal was justified in making those observations was not considered by the High Court. [ 432 E ] (iv) The High Courts have taken a view that the decisions of this Court are binding on all courts and tribunals. [ 433 D ] (v) There is no indication in the judgment of the High court that the decision in the Bombay region at least there is a general agree ment that the normal rule of retirement will be that the employee concerned must be retired at the end of the previous year. [ 434 C ] (vi) The contention that the High Courts order was wrong because the Tribunal has ignored the earlier orders passed by the Government which had been accepted by the parties before it.

The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1961 and was registered as a private limited company under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. On May 19, 1965 the Company Law Board passed an order of winding up of the appellant company. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the said order on the ground that it had been made mala fide by the Chairman of the Board and not by the Managing Director or any other person who was acting as the Managing director. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the order of the Chairman was bad because he did not give notice to the appellant and that the resolution was invalid. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The power of the Company Judge under section 235 is discretionary and the court has no jurisdiction to interfere with the discretion exercised by him. [ 320 C ] (2) The powers conferred on the Company Court by section 234 are wide enough to be exercised only when there is a violation of the principles of natural justice. It cannot be said that the power of superintendence over the affairs of the company is vested in the Chairman and not in the Managing Directors. [ 321 F G ] (3) The appellant's contention that the impugned order was vitiated by fraud and mis feas ance is without merit. The fact that the appellant was appointed as Managing Director of the respondent company does not make the order illegal. [ 322 B ] (4) The order of termination of the agreement dated May 19. 1964 was void as it was made without jurisdiction. [ 323 D ] (5) The question whether the order terminating the agreement was valid or not must depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. If the order was passed by the Board of Directors of the Respondent company, the same could have been challenged in the High Courts. [ 324 E ] (6) The High Courts were right in holding that since the order dated May 20, 1965 was passed under the influence of the Minister of Finance, the order would be invalid. [ 325 A ] (7) The action taken by the appellant in the present case was not for the purpose of preventing the appellant from taking steps in accordance with law.

The appellants were convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months. They filed a petition in this Court challenging their conviction and sentence. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) There is no evidence that the appellants had any common intention with the daco its to commit dacoity or that they had committed theft of stolen property. [ 721 F ] (2) The fact that the accused persons were not identified as daco its was not disputed. It is also not possible to say that there was no other evidence to show that the culprits were actually involved in the dacoity. [ 722 B C ] (3) The offence was committed at night when the dacoity took place. The circumstances do not admit of the drawing of the presumption in the case.

The petitioners were the owners of a factory in which they had been manufacturing and selling certain articles. They filed writ petitions before this Court challenging the validity of Section 5 of the Act, on the ground that it was not an essential commodity within the meaning of section 2 (x) of the, as it was found to be adulter ated by the State Government under the provisions of the Delhi Po isons Rules, 1926. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the notification did not suffer from any infirmity. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The provisions of Section 2 are not hit by any cons ti t ution al limitation. [ 225 F ] 2. The object of the enactment is to regulate the import, possession and sale of po isons. It is also not necessary that the same substance should be declared as poison for the entire country. The purpose of the legislation is to prevent the use of the same for the purpose of committing murder or mischief by poison ing cattle. [ 226 E ] 3. The word'poison'has been defined in section 2 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, to mean " poison ". The definition of poison is very wide and includes poison. The term'poison ', therefore, cannot be construed to include poison. [ 227 B C ] 4. The words'poison '.'have been used in the definition of'poison in section 5 of Act, 19 04, and the expression'poison has been used therein. The definition is inclusive and not exhaustive.

The assessee, a firm registered under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1952 53. In the assessment proceedings for the years 1953 54 and 1954 55, the assessee claimed deduction of Rs. 2, 68, 385 / as bad debt due from it in respect of its business dealings with the Bombay firm. The Income Tax Officer disallowed this claim on the ground that the money lent by the assessee to the Bombay company was not a loan made in the ordinary course of its money lending business. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax officer but allowed the appeal filed by the Revenue. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that the sum of Rs 2, 67, 385 /- was not an " amount " which could be deducted from the profits of the assessee's business. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The question whether the sum received by the appellant in the present case is a " loan " within the meaning of section 10 (2)( xi) of the Indian In com et ax Act, 1961, must be answered in the affirmative and against the assessee. [ 423 C ] (2) The Tribunal has found that the monies sent by the respondent were not loans made in ordinary course or in the course of the business of the appellant. It is true that the Tribunal has come to certain ab rupt conclusions, but all the t ame it cannot be denied that the findings reached by the tribunal are findings of fact and those findings are supported by the evidence on record. [ 424 F G ] (3) The High Court erred in holding that the amounts paid by the asses see to the Madras firm were not " loans made " in the normal course of their business. [ 425 B ] (4) The finding of the Tribunal that the moneys sent by assessee to Bombay firm were " loans " made in " the ordinary sense of the word " loan ", is based on no material. [ 426 D ] (5) The conclusion arrived at by the Tribunal is correct.

The petitioners in the Special Leave Petitions were the owners of certain lands acquired by the State Government under the Land Acquisition Act. They filed applications before the Land Acqu is tion Officer for determination of compensation and also for grant of interim stay of dispossession. The Land Acquisition Officer rejected their applications on the ground that they had not been made within two years from the date of publication of the declaration under Section 4 of the Land acquisition Act, 1894. The petitioners challenged the order of the High Court in a writ petition which was dismissed by a Division Bench of the Karnataka High Court on November 29, 1988. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the High Courts have erred in law in holding that the award was not made within the stipulated time. Dismis sing the special leave petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court has rightly held that the awards were not made beyond the period of two years as contemplated by section 11 A of the Act. [ 823 B ] 2. The question whether the award should be made within one year from the publication of declaration under section 4 of Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1984, is a matter of policy. It is well settled that the relief under Article 136 of the Constitution is discretionary and a petitioner who approaches this Court for such relief must come with fr ank and full disclosure of facts. If he fails to do so and sup press es material facts, his application is liable to be dismissed. [ 824 C D ] 3. The fact of the stay orders being un available, the petitioners are liable to make good the loss caused to them.

The appellant bank was a banking company. It had its branches in the State of Bombay and it was governed by the Sas try Award as modified by the Labour Appellate Tribunal. In the year 1962, the appellant bank had been paying to its employees at Rs. 190 per month as on January 1, 1959. On January 1. 1962, an award was made under section 33 (2) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the award. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the award did not set aside the award but directed payment of bonus for the period from January 1,. 1959 to December 31, 1949. The Bank appealed to this Court. Held: (i) The award of the labour court was correct; (ii) the award of bonus was given effect to only after the basic pay was worked out as on April 1, 1949, and therefore, the award could not be said to have been passed beyond that date. The award was not open to challenge because the award was based on the provisions of the Sas ty Award which were applicable to the case. (iii) The appellant had no right to claim any increments under sub cl. (d) of cl. 5. The question whether the appellant was entitled to any increment under sub clause (d), or not, was not considered by the High court.

The appellants, who were the owners of a hotel, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notices issued by the Chief Minister. They contended that they had been given a right to be heard before the issue of the notice and that their rights could not be affected by the issuance of the said notices. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellants'claim was barred by limitation. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the notices were invalid as they did not comply with the requirements of section 5 (1) of the Act. Dismis sing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) The appellants have no case that the notice was bad because they did so under section 5 of the Indian Telegraph Act. [ 280 F ] (ii) The question whether the notices are void or void able is a matter which can be decided only after an enquiry into the allegations made against the person concerned. If the allegations are found to be correct, the court will have to decide whether there is any violation of fundamental rights. But if the allegations do not disclose any cause of action, the Court would not normally interfere. [ 281 B C ] (iii) The High Courts should not ordinarily interfere with the discretion exercised by the authorities unless the reasons for such decision are clearly stated. It is not necessary to give detailed reasons why the decisions of the Government are vitiated by mala fides or extraneous considerations. [ 282 G H; 283 A ] (iv) The principles of natural justice must be read into the provisions of the statute. The rules of natural Justice must be complied with in letter and spirit. [ 284 D ] (v) The rule of audi alteram partem has its own limits and is a part of the rule of law. It cannot be put in a stra it jacket formula. It has to be applied with care and caution. [ 285 E ] (vi) The principle of audi alter em partem is applicable to all cases where the order is passed without giving any hearing or opportunity of being heard. The principles are well settled.

The respondent was a partner in a firm carrying on business as grain and other goods. He had been doing the business of lending money to his son, who was also a partner of the firm. In the assessment year 1957 58 he made a gift of Rs. 50, 000 to his wife and grand sons. The Income Tax Officer held that the gifts were valid gifts but allowed the deduction under section 12 (1) of the Act. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax officer. The Tribunal held that there was no valid gift. The High Court in second appeal held that since the gift was not proved, it could not be said that the gift did not operate to bring into existence a valid gift and therefore, the gift must be deemed to have been made in favour of the assessee. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The gift is not valid gifts even though there is no acceptance of the gift by the done e. [ 128 D ] (ii) The question whether the gift is valid or not does not arise because the donor has no over draft facility with any bank. It is not necessary for the purpose of making a gift. [ 129 E F ] (iii) The fact that the donor had a full share in the partnership property would not make him liable to tax. [ 130 G ] (iv) The High court was right in holding that the Gift was not valid. [ 131 C ] (v) The Gift was invalid because the gift had not been properly made. The gift was void able. [ 132 B ] (vi) The amount of Rs 1, 50, 00, which was paid by the deceased to his daughter was not sufficient to show that the done es were not the owners of the property. [ 133 H; 134 A ] (vii) The income tax authorities were wrong in treating the gift as valid gift because the done ee had not retained the possession and enjoyment of the gifted property. The Gift is not invalid.

The High Court of Orissa, in exercise of its power under article 235 of the Constitution, has framed rules for regulating the conditions of service of persons appointed to the civil posts. Rule 2 (1) of the Orissa Su perior Judicial Service Rules 1963 provides that " All appointments to the service shall be made by the Governor and shall be subject to the approval of the Governor ". Rule 3 (1)( a) of these rules provides that every appointment to the post of district judge or class I Judge shall be on probation for a period not exceeding three years. The proviso to this rule states that if any officer is appointed as district judge he shall not be entitled to hold any office in the secret ari at unless he holds such an appointment. In other words, the appointing authority may appoint him to offic iate in any post in the confidential category. But it does not mean that the Government can appoint a person to offic iated in the administrative post. The High court was right in holding that the State Government could not have posted them to administrative posts in the regular line of promotion. The order of the High Court directing the government to fill up the vacancies was set aside. The appellant's contention that the High court should have directed the government not to make any appointment to any post was rejected. The respondent contended that the government had no power to appoint a District Judge and that the power to transfer judges from one department to another was only with the consent of the Government. Held, that the order of transfer was valid and the High Courts were right in quashing the order. The power to issue directions to the government was wide enough to include the power of transferring judges from the courts subordinate to the district courts. It was open to the High courts to fix the period during which they would hold any executive post. There was nothing in the Act to show that the legislature intended to confer powers on the High Judges to transfer officers from one cadre to another. The word'control'in section 2 (i) of Act No. 23 of 1951 means the power exercisable by the High. Court to transfer a particular officer from one post to another within the same cadre. The expression'control ', in section 4 (1), means the control over the subordinate judiciary. The words'control '. are defined in section 3 (c) of that Act. The definition of'control " in section 5 (1). includes disciplinary jurisdiction as well as disciplinary action. The Government cannot be said to have delegated its power to the Chief Justice to appoint the judges of the Supreme Court. The Chief Justice of the Patna High Court was not competent to appoint any Judge of the Calcutta High Court.

The appellant, a co sharer of the land in question, filed a suit for partition and separate possession of his share. The trial court decreed the suit on the ground that the appellant had no right to pre empt the sale by virtue of section 15 (1)( b) of the Act. On appeal, the High Court held that the right of pre emption was not absolute but only a limited interest in favour of the co sharers. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the expression'other co sharers'in clause fourth ly of section 14 (1) (b) must be read as including all the co owners who are entitled to pre emption under clause fourth ed to the exclusion of the vendors. Dismis sing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The word'other'in cl. fourth ly means'other ', which is not intended to exclude the co sharer from the scope of clause fourth. [ 128 D ] 2. The expression'others'in section 15 of the, cannot be construed to mean'other persons '. The use of the expression " other co owners " in clause fifth ly of Section 15 (l)( b), makes it clear that the legislature wanted to exclude any co sharer also from the purview of clause sixth ly of s. 15 (I)( b). [ 129 E F ] 3. The words'other Co sharers'used in clause third ly of sub section (1), namely,'other non sharers'would include'other members'and'other such co sharers '. The expression " Other co sharers " in section 16 (1 (b), therefore, does not include the co - sharers. [ 130 G H; 131 A B ] 4. The right of the pre emption to co sharers is held to be inter se co sharers and not to deny the right to the pre empt or to enjoy the right in the property. [ 132 C ] 5. The power to grant a right of re pres en tation to the co co sharers has been conferred on the appellant by section 15. [ 133 D ] 6. The appellant having failed to comply with the provisions of section 25 (1). he could not claim the right under clause Fourth ly of the section.

The appellant, a Hindu undivided family, was the owner of certain properties. He had filed a suit for partition and separate possession of his share in the property. The trial Court decreed the suit on the ground that the sale deeds were not binding upon him as they were executed by the father and his two sons who were minors at the time of the sale. On appeal, the High Court held that the alien ees had no interest in the properties and that the alienation made by them was valid and the trans fere es had become owners of the property and that they had become entitled to recover the amount from the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the compromise decree was void because the parties had agreed to settle all equ ities between the parties and that there was no agreement or settlement between the father, and the appellant's brother and the same was not binding on the appellant and that therefore the sale deed could not be acted upon. Dismis sing the appeal, HELD: 1. The compromise petition is genuine and lawful. It is not possible to accept the contention that the said alien ee has no interest whatsoever in the said property. [ 543 B ] 2. The alien ees have no interest, in the subject matter of the suit, and are not bound to account for mesne profits. They have no right created under the alleged sale deeds. Their possession is without authority of law. Even if the compromise is valid and legal, the same has to be acted on. [ 544 C D ] 3. The alienation is invalid and cannot be acted thereupon. [ 545 E F ] 4. The gift deed is not valid and none of the alien ee can claim any benefit under the said document. [ 546 G ] 5. The transaction is not illegal and cannot bind the parties. The sale deeds are subsequent to 21. 8. 1987. The parties have signed the compromise. The terms of the compromise are not binding. [ 547 A ] 6. The fact that there is a dispute about the payment of Rs. 1 lakh to Sudarshan Gupta does not make any difference. The consideration money is not paid by the alien ors. [ 548 H; 549 A ] 7. The recitals in the compromise deed clearly show that the parties have accepted the same and have also admitted that the other properties are not covered by the sale agreements.

The appellants, who were the workmen of the two companies, filed applications under section 49 of the. The Tribunal held that the provisions of the Act had been complied with and that the benefit of sick leave was available to them in the case of a period of three days from December 14, 1969, as provided by the proviso to section 49 (1) of the, and that they were entitled to the benefits of the sick leave for the first two days only. In appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Tribunal had committed an error in holding that the appellants were not entitled to any relief because the sick Leave granted to them was not admissible to them. Dismis sing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The question whether the benefit should be given to the workmen in the cases of sickness leave is a matter which has to be decided on the facts of each case. [ 10 E ] 2. The appellants have not been able to show that the awards in question are illegal or unjust. They have not made out any case for interference. [ 11 C D ] 3. The award in the present case is based on the pay scales of the employees of the three companies. It is clear that the workmen's demand for sick leave has been denied by the Tribunal. [ 12 F G ] 4. The appellant company has also not been shown to have been employed in the factory at Baroda. The fact that the Company has been paying the wages for the period of the strike cannot be said to be relevant for the purpose of determining the amount of sick allowance. [ 13 B ] 5. The contention that the benefits under the Act could not be extended to the workers of the Company is without substance. The workmen have been given the benefit under the scheme of the benefits admissible under the statute. The benefit of the scheme must be allowed to the employees in the same manner as the workmen. [ 15 H; 16 A ] 6. The Industrial Tribunal has considered the entire scheme of rehabilitation and the benefit granted to the concerned workmen. The High Court has rightly pointed out that the scheme does not cover all contingencies of sickness, and in any event the first proviso to Section 49 of The Employees State Insurance Act, 1948, applies to the factories in the State of Gujarat. [ 17 B ] 7. The scheme of these Acts clearly shows that the Scheme of the benefit would be available to the workman in the circumstances of the case. The benefits under those Acts can be availed of only if the conditions laid down therein are satisfied. [ 18 B ] 8. The Scheme of these enactments do not provide for any special treatment to the retrenched workmen. If the workmen are not paid the benefits, the workmen will get the benefit. [ 19 E ] 9.

The appellant was detained under the provisions of section 3 (1) of the, and on his being arrested he was served with a notice to show cause why he should not be detained. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the detention order contending that the grounds were vague and that the detaining authority had no power to make such an order as the detaining Authority did not apply its mind to the question whether or not the grounds are vague. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the ground of vag u eness was not sufficient to justify the detention. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the order of detention was mala fide because the detaining authorities had failed to consider the fact that the detenu was given adequate particulars and that there was nothing to indicate that the subjective satisfaction of the detaining officer was based on extraneous considerations. Held: (i) The contention that the right to be furnished particulars is subject to the limitation under article 22 (5) must be rejected. The words " shall be supplied " in the sub clause (6) of article 22 must be read in the context of the constitutional right guaranteed by article 22. It is only when the requirement of the law is satisfied that the detention is necessary for the purpose of preventing the detenu from acting in any manner prejudicial to the security of the State or the maintenance of public order, that the obligation to furnish particulars is imposed upon the detenu. The expression " shall not be supplied to him " in article 22 means that the authority making the order has to communicate to the detenu the grounds on which the order is made and also to afford him the earliest opportunity of making a representation against the order. If the order does not contain any such provision, the order would be invalid.

The respondent was a commissioned officer in the Indian Army. He was tried by a court mar tial for an offence under section 19 of the, read with r. 14 of the Army Rules 1954. The trial judge convicted him and sentenced him to suffer rigorous imprisonment for one year and to pay a fine of Rs. 1, 000. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence from two years to three months'rigorous imprisonment. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the provisions of the Act were ultra vires the; (ii) the order of removal was not passed by the Central Government as required by section 191 (2)( a) of the. Dismis sing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The words " subject to the provisions Of the Act " occurring in section 19 make section 19 wholly inapplicable to the case. [ 450 B ] (2) Section 19 is not ultra vires because it is not necessary to refer to the other provisions of section 19 which are similar to those contained in section 18 of the read with rule 14 of Army Rules, 1954. [ 451 C D ] (3) The word " subject " in section 15 of the said Act means " subject only to the provision of the rules made thereunder ". It does not mean that the Central Govt. has no power to remove a person from service.

The appellant was a Panchayat Samiti. On June 1, 1959 the Panchayat passed resolution to levy octroi duty on the goods brought by it from its own sources in the State of Madhya Pradesh. The appellant challenged the validity of the resolution and the demand for payment of octroi duty. The High Court held that the Panchayat had no power to impose octroi duty under r. 21 of the Rules. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The words " any tax or fee " in r. 5 must be read as " any other tax or fees ". [ 222 E ] (ii) The word " taxes " is not defined in the Act but is used in the sense of " taxes ", which means taxes imposed or levied by the Government. It is true that the word " Taxes " has been used in a wide sense in the context of the Act and the rules made thereunder. But the word'taxes'is not capable of being construed in a narrow sense so as to include all taxes or fees. [ 223 F G ] (iii) The expression " taxes or fee ", in r, 3 (b), means taxes or cess es. The word'tax'is generally used in contrad ist in ction with the word tax. The term " tax " is normally used in an inclusive sense. The meaning of the word is not restricted to taxes or duties. The dictionary meaning of " tax or duty " is also not very clear. The use of the words " taxes, fees, etc., " in the definition of " taxation " shows that the tax is not a tax or a fee.

The appellants were employed as workmen in the respondent company. They were dismissed from service by an order of the Conciliation Officer on December 31, 1951. On January 17, 1952, the appellant No. 1 filed a petition under section 33 (1) read with section 33 A of the Act for quashing the proceedings and for a direction to the respondent to reinstate them. The High Court allowed the petition holding that the conciliation proceedings could not be continued after 14 days but only terminated because the conciliation proceeding was pending before the Conciliation officer. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the provisions of section 20 (2)( b) of the, did not apply to the case since the conciliation was not completed within 14 days of the commencement of the conciliation Proceedings. Held: (i) The contention that the termination of the proceedings was deemed to take place when the report is received by the appropriate Government cannot be accepted. Section 12 (6) of The Act provides that where a settlement is arrived at, when the Report of the Advisory Board is received or if the Conciliation Office is not closed, the report shall be made and the proceedings closed within a week or if no settlement is reached, when a report is sent by the Conciliation Of fi cer to the appropriate government. The words " pendency of conciliation proceedings " are wide enough to include the time during which the report has been received by him. The word'pendency'in section 12 (3) of that Act means the date of receipt of the report by the conciliation officer. The expression " pendency " in section 20 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, does not mean that the reference must be made within 14 months of the date when the final report is submitted. The scheme of the section shows that the period of 15 days is intended to be computed from the date on which the reports are received by a Conciliation Officer. The fact that the Conciliation Officers have delayed the submission of their report is not relevant. The termination of conciliation proceeding is deemed to have taken place when a memorandum of the settlement is signed by the parties. The conciliation proceedings do not cease to be one merely because they are in the present case. The Labour Court had held that the delay in making the award was due to the circumstances beyond its control. The question whether the conciliation should be continued or not was not considered. The decision of the High Court was reversed by this Court.

The petitioner was detained under the provisions of the, and he was served with a detention order. He challenged his detention on various grounds including that there was no cogent material before the detaining authority to justify his detention. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the detenu had not been given any opportunity to make an effective representation against the detention order and that the grounds of detention were vague and indefinite. Allow ing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The grounds for forming the satisfaction for the need for the detention are irrelevant and must be read as such. [ 910 E ] 2. The fact that the petitioner was in custody is not relevant because it is not stated that the detaining officer was satisfied that the detention was necessary for putting him back in jail. It is also not shown that the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authorities was based on extraneous considerations or irrelevant considerations. [ 911 F G ] 3. The power of preventive detention should not be exercised unless the circumstances mentioned in section 3 (2) of the Act have been fully considered. [ 912 B C ] 4. The facts of this case show that the order of detention was passed on the basis of the materials placed before the Advisory Board. There was no indication that the said order was not passed in accordance with law. [ 913 D ] 5. The order of preventive bail could not be justified merely because the detaining Authority was satisfied about the necessity of the detention. [ 914 A ] 6. The question whether the order was valid or not has to be decided on the facts and circumstances of each case. [ 915 H ] 7. In the instant case, the order dated 2nd January 1986 was passed after the expiry of the period of detention. There is nothing to indicate that the Detaining Authority was aware of the fact that there were no imminent possibility of his being released. [ 918 B ] 8. The detention order was made on the ground that the activities of the detenu were prejudicial to the maintenance of public order. The detaining authority was therefore, justified in making the order. [ 919 E ] 9. The impugned order of the High Court is set aside.

The appellant, a dealer in gold and silver ornaments, was carrying on business as a money lender. He filed an application under section 28 of the Gold Control Act for the grant of a license to him to carry on money lending, banking or any other business in the same premises in which he carried on business. The Assistant Collector of Central Excise issued a show cause notice to the appellant who contended that the provisions of the Act were not applicable to his case because the object of the enactment was to prevent the circum ven tion of the other provisions of law and that the said provision was violative of article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the appellant's contention that the restrictions imposed by section 28 were unreasonable and un canal ised and that they were violative of articles 14 and 19 (1) (g) of the constitution was unsustainable. In appeal to this Court it was contended that: (i) the restriction imposed by the section was excessive and unreasonable; (ii) the expression " reasonable opportunity " used in sec. 28 did not mean adequate guidance to the Administrator in the matter of exercising his discretion under that section; and (iii) the section conferred a very wide and vague power on the Administrator to refuse permission to carry out the business as such. Dismis sing the appeal, HELD: (1)( a) The policy and purpose of the statute are to be found in sections 28 and 29 of the. [ 10 B ] (b) The scheme of the section is that the legislature has given wide powers to the administrator to grant or renew a license for a particular area or class of goods. It may be mentioned that the section does not provide for any objective standard or norm but only lays down the guidelines for the exercise of the power. The section does provide for the maximum number of dealers existing in the region. [ 11 C D ] (2) The object of enacting section 28 is to ensure prevention of circum ven tions of the various classes of persons specified therein. The object is to enable the authorities to give wide powers or discretion to the executive authority. The power to refuse or renew licences is conferred upon the Administrator. The words " reasonable grounds " have been used in section 28. The word'reasonable'has been used to indicate the nature of the restrictions. [ 12 E F ] (3) The expression'reasonable opportunity'means adequate guidance for the purpose of making the order. The expression " sufficient reason " has been employed in section 27 (6) to convey the idea of the reasons for the belief. [ 13 G H ] (4) The section cannot be struck down on the ground of excessive delegation of legislative power.

The appellants, who were the trustees of a temple in the village of the respondent, filed a suit for possession of certain properties and claimed that they had been appointed as trustees by the respondent No. 4, who was the manager of the temple. The trial court decreed the suit on the ground that the appellants had failed to prove their title to the property and that the properties belonged to the temple and that they were not the owners of the properties. On appeal, the High Court held that the plaintiffs had established their claim of adverse possession against the respondent Nos. 1 to 3, but dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the suit was barred under article 134 B of the Limitation Act; (ii) that the suit could not be maintained because the appellants'predecessor had died long before the institution of the suit and therefore, the suit should have been dismissed; and (iii) that even if the suit had been instituted after 12 years from the date of the death of the original trustee, the same would not be barred under section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Held: (i). The suit was within time. The suit must fail. It is well settled that where a person has no right to sue or defend his own legal representative, he cannot be sued by the defendant. (ii). The question whether a suit is barred by limitation depends upon the facts proved in the case. If the plaintiff succeeds in establishing his right, the question whether the suit is within time does not arise.

The appellant, a partnership firm, was carrying on the business of constructing cinema theatre in the premises of the respondent No. 1 and other shops in the said building. In the course of its business, the appellant had taken a licence from the District Magistrate under section 3 of the Act for running a Cinema Theatre. On July 22, 1966, the District magistrate issued a notice to the appellant calling upon him to show cause why he should not be suspended or revoked as the case may be, by an order dated November 16, 1967. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the said notice. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant was entitled to have his licence renewed in accordance with the provisions of the law. The Division Bench held that the impugned order was violative of the principles of natural justice inasmuch as it did not give any opportunity to the petitioner to make his representation against the proposed action. Allow ing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) The High court erred in holding that there was no obligation on the part of the District Magistrates to give a notice or hearing to the firm or its partners before he passed the impugned orders. [ 594 B ] (ii) The power to suspend a licence is conferred only by Section 6 F of the Bombay Cin emato graph Act, 1955. It does not vest in the District Collector the power to take all steps necessary for effective enforcement of the statute. The power of revocation and unless the conditions precedent mentioned in the section are present, the licensing authority has no jurisdiction to pass the impugned Order. [ 595 C D ] (iii) The order of suspension of the licence issued in respect of the Theatre cannot be said to have been made without a licence in contravention of the provisions contained in the Act and the Rules. [ 596 G H; 597 A ] (iv) The impugned order is one passed by the District Judge in the exercise of his function of administering the provision of the Statute. The impugned Order is therefore, invalid.

The appellants were the lessees of a factory in which they had been granted leases by the Custodian under section 12 (1) of the, and the respondent was declared to be the lessee. On the question whether the lease was void or not, HELD: (i) The respondent was acting within his authority in issuing Exhibit C in so far as it concerned the lease granted in favour of the appellants. It was open to him to cancel the lease if he was aggrieved by the order of the Custodian. [ 983 G H ] (ii) The provisions of section 12 of the Act are intended to apply only to leases granted by the evacuee and not to leases made by the Central Government. The respondent could not be said to have been authorised to cancel a lease in respect of the property belonging to the appellants, because the respondent did not make any such application. The appellants'contention that the notice was invalid on the ground that the respondent had no power under section 10 of the. is not correct. The section merely says that the Custodian has the power to cancel an agreement to sell the mills and the factory to them, but does not include any contract between the parties. [ 984 E F; 988 A B ] (iii) Section 12 of Act XXX I of 1950, provides that where the Custodian is satisfied that there is a breach of the conditions of the lease, the Custodian may, after giving the parties reasonable opportunity of being heard, cancel the licence. In the present case, the respondent could have exercised the power under s. 12 of that Act.

The appellant was a minor son of the deceased. He filed an application under section 230 of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955 for setting aside the order dated 6th August, 1977 passed by the Sub Divisional Officer on the ground that he had not been given any opportunity to adduce additional evidence in support of his claim and that the ceiling area should be determined according to old law i. e. Act of 1955 and not according to the new law i.. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Board had no jurisdiction to set aside the orders of the Sub divisional Officer and the Revenue Appellate Authority. In appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the power of general superintendence vested in the Board could not be exercised by the Board as the sub Divisional Officer had committed an error of law in determining the ceiling limit of the land under the Act of 1973. Dismis sing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Section 221 of the Act is not subject to the other provisions of the Constitution. It is only administrative as well as judicial powers. [ 728 E ] 2. The power of the Board to make its own rules or directions has been conferred by the Act. The Board has wide powers to issue such directions and the power to revise the same cannot be delegated to the Board. The State Government has power to exercise its powers of superintendence over all revenue courts and it does not apply to judicial proceedings. [ 729 B C ] 3. The High court did not go into the merits of the controversy nor it went into the question whether the power was properly exercised by subordinate courts. [ 730 D ] 4. The decision of the Division Bench of the High Court in the case of K ana and others vs Board of Revenue, Rajasthan, AIR 19 16 Pat. 292 (F. B.) relied upon by the appellant is not applicable to the present case because the said decision was rendered in the peculiar facts of the case. [ 731 G H;

The appellant, a public limited company, was carrying on the business of printing and publishing newspapers. It had been engaged in the production or publication of news print. The appellant's case was that it was an ed itor ial comment ary made by the 1st respondent in its publication of the newspaper. The 1st respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the said order. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant was not entitled to any relief under article 226 of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The expression " newspaper " as defined in section 2 (d) of the Act means a newspaper which is published either generally or specially in relation to the publication of a newspaper. [ 779 B ] (2) The word " newspaper ", as used in the definition of " newspaper'in section 3 (c) of that Act includes a newspaper, a newspaper or periodical, a mag az ine containing news, and a newspaper; and the expression " news " in section 13 A of the Indian Penal Code has to be construed in the light of the context in which it occurs. [ 780 G H ] (3) The words " news paper " are wide enough to cover the public ations of both the sides of the paper and the public. The expression'news'is not defined in the Act but is a broad one. The dictionary meaning of the word'news ', as given in the Shor ter Oxford English Dictionary, is " news ". The dictionary gives the meaning of news as " news of news ". [ 781 D E ] (4) The term'news " is not sy non y mous with the word " news '. The dictionary meanings of the expression'newspaper'as understood in the Web ster's New International Dictionary, referred to.

The appellant was a tenant of the respondent. He filed an ejectment petition under section 41 of the Bombay Rent Act, 1958 against the respondent for possession of the premises on the ground that he had been in occupation of the suit premises since 1st September 1965 and that he was not liable to be evicted from the said premises. The trial court dismissed the eviction petition but the High Court allowed the revision application holding that the respondent was a licensee and not a tenant. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the agreement between the parties was a lease and not licence and therefore the respondent could not be evicted under section 21 (1) of the Act. Dismis sing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The expression " licence " is used in section 5 (4A) of Bombay Rent Control Act, 1947 which provides that if any person has acquired any right or interest in any property, whether before or after the commencement of the tenancy, such right shall not be deemed to have been transferred by reason only of his being a licensee. [ 10 69 B ] 2. Section 6 (4) of Maharashtra Act 17 of 1973 makes it clear that the landlord who has a subsisting agreement with a tenant or a licensee shall not terminate the agreement unless the tenant pays to the landlord the rent payable by him. It is clear from the language of section 6 (4A), that the intention of the parties is clear that there is no question of estoppel against the landlord. [ 11 71 F G ] 3. The object of the legislature in enacting section 5 is to provide a remedy to the tenants who are entitled to use the premises for their own purpose. If they do not want to continue in occupation, then the provision of section 15A would apply.

The appellant was a resident of the former State of Rajasthan. He had been granted a licence for export of certain goods and in pursuance thereof he exported them to the Government of India. On the basis of the said licence, the appellant applied for and obtained a licence under the Indian Ex er cise Act, 1947, from the Government. The appellant claimed refund of the amount paid by him on account of the import duty payable on the goods. The claim was rejected by the Central Government. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the agreement between the Rul er of the erstwhile State of Jaipur and the Maharaja of Jodhpur was not a law within the meaning of article 295 (2) of the Constitution; (2). that the agreement did not have any recognition of the liability of the Rul ers of the two States which came into existence after August 15, 1947; and (3) that the appellant could not be treated as an " existing law " within the definition of section 2 (1)( d) of that Act. Held: (i) that there was no recognition of liability by the new sovereign and the appellant was entitled to refund of its tax paid on the basis that the liability arose only when the contract was entered into and the liability was discharged. (ii) that even if the contract of the appellant with the Rul ing State of Jodhpur continued to exist, the liability to pay the tax would still remain un affected and the appellants were not liable to refund the amount of tax collected in advance. (iii) that in view of the fact that the contract with the Government was not one of the contracting parties, the payment of the tax was not valid.

The appellants were the owners of a rice mill. They had been carrying on business in cotton and ground nut oil, but they did not pay any amount to the respondent as their sales tax was not paid by them. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the Act and the Rules framed thereunder. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the provisions of the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939, were ultra vires the State Legislature. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that (1) the Act was bad because the Act did not provide for the levy of a tax at all; (2) the levy was invalid because the legislature had no power to impose a tax on the sale or purchase of goods; (3) the imposition of a penalty under section 14 of the was illegal because the provision contained in section 5 (4)( a) of the said Act was void because the section itself provided that the Commissioner could make an order imposing a penalty which he could not do if the Act had not been passed; and (4) the impugned Act was violative of article 19 (1)( g) of Constitution. Held: (i) that the Act is valid because the definition of'dealer'given in section 2 (j) of that Act includes a person who carries on the business of buying and selling goods and the word " dealer " in section 14 means only a person whose name has been entered in the register maintained by the Commissioner under the Act. The words " dealer ", " dealer, " and " dealer'are wide enough to include a person other than a dealer. The expression " dealer ". in section 15 of the Bombay Sales Tax Acts, 1946, does not mean a person, who is liable to pay tax under the Central Provinces and Ber ar Sales Tax, Act, 1947, but is a dealer within the meaning of section 2 of the Central Sales Tax. The word " person " in the context of section 14 must be construed in its ordinary sense and not in a narrow way. The term " dealer," in section 16 of the Indian Income Tax Act is not sy non y mous with the word'dealer '. It is used in the Act in the sense of a person being a dealer in respect of certain commodities. A dealer is not a dealer under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941, and therefore, the Act cannot be held to be unconstitutional.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed his conviction but reduced the sentence of death to imprisonment for life. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) there was no evidence of any prior meeting or a meeting of minds; (2) that the accused had not been charged with an offence under section 326 of the I. P. C., and (3) that he was guilty of murder. Held: (i) that in the present case, the prosecution has failed to prove that the appellant was guilty under section 307 of the Penal Code. (ii) that there is no evidence to show that the deceased was assaulted by the appellant and that the injuries were caused by him only because he was a member of the family. (iii) that even if the prosecution could establish that the appellants were members of the unlawful assembly, they must be held to have committed the offence of murder within the meaning of section 302 read with section 34 of the IPC. (iv) that as the prosecution did not prove that there was a common intention between the two persons, the conviction of the appellants should be altered from one under section 304 Part II to section 325 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

The petitioner was appointed as a Section Officer in the Central Public Works Department on 22. 10. 1947 and he was promoted to offic iate as Assistant Engineer in Class I service with effect from 5. 11. 1976. He was reverted to his substantive post of Assistant Engineer on 25. 5. 1954, but he was reverted back to his original post on 29. 2. 1980. On 3. 7. 1961, he was again promoted as officiating Executive Engineer in class II service. In the meantime, the Government of India issued an order dated 8. 10, 1955, whereby the petitioner was reverted from the post of Deputy Chief Engineer to the post which he held prior to the date of his compulsory retirement. The petitioner challenged the said order by filing Writ Petition No. 73 of 1966 before this Court. This Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the order of compulsory retirement and directed that the petitioner would be entitled to draw salary and allowances admissible under the rules. The petitioners were also given the benefit of the order dated 4. 9. 1965 passed by the Government. The respondents filed Special Leave Petitions against the judgment of the High Court. The Supreme Court dismissed the Special Leave Petition. Allow ing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The ratio of the decision in Tah ili ani's case is not correct and sub clause (i) of Rule 56 (j) applies to the facts of the present case. [ 62 B ] 2. The purpose of Fundamental Rules 56 (k) is to classify Government servants into two categories and sub clauses (i), (ii) and (iii) has a purpose behind it. If the con di tion indicated in sub clause is to treat the Government servant in Class II or Class II service or post, whether substantively, temporarily or on officiating basis. It is obvious that the purpose of the rule is to confer power on the appropriate authority to compulsorily retire Government servant. Therefore, the contention of the petitioner that the impugned order is violative of Article 14 of the Constitution is rejected. [ 63 C D ] 3. The object of Fundamental Rule 56 is to abol ish all Government servants who at the relevant time are in Class III or Class IV service or posts. The intention of the Government is to exclude those Government servants from the purview of sub clause. [ 64 G H; 65 A ] 4. The words " if he is in Class V or Class I or Class III service or Post " occurring in sub cl.( i) mean " in Class 1 or Class 2 service or the post ", and the word " shall " does not include the Government servants in Class 11 or Class 11 service or in Class IV services or post. [ 66 E F ] 5. The expression " in any other case " in sub clauses 2 (i)( ii) of Clause (j), means " in the case of a person who is in the service or pay scale ". The word " may " in Sub clause (ii), means in the context of the provision of the statute, the word'may'in the proviso, means " where the person is in class I or class II Service or post." [ 67 E F ]. 6. The word'shall'in sub section (i). means'in relation to'the service '. The word used in sub - clause (iv) is'in respect of'and'in'in other cases'means'to'in any case '. The meaning of the word in sub Clause (i); is that the Government Servant is in such service or grade or post and he had entered into service before attaining the age of 35 years.

The appellant Corporation, a public sector undertaking, was the owner of certain insurance policies. The deceased had taken a policy for Rs. 50, 000 / and his wife died on December 13, 1960. The widow of the deceased filed a suit in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Mas ul ipat am against the Life Insurance Corporation and its officers for recovery of the amount due to her under the two policies. In the suit the respondents contended that the proposal was not accepted by the Divisional Manager as he had no authority to accept it and that the claim was not settled. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed the decree. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The High Court was right in holding that there was no concluded contract between the deceased and the Life Assurance Corporation and that there is no concluded agreement between the parties. (ii) The life assured had been paid only half of the premium and therefore the question of acceptance did not arise. (iii) The expression " under writing " sign if ies acceptance. It means acceptance of the proposal. (iv) The word'under writing'sign if es an acceptance. The words " under write " sign ify acceptance. (v) The term " under written " sign ified acceptance by the parties or from which the law raises a presumption of acceptance. [ 352 B D ] (vi) The words'under write'sign ify the acceptance of proposal. The word " under writer " sign ifying acceptance must be signed by some act or acts agreed on by the party to whom an offer is made. If the person to whom the offer is given accepts it unconditionally and communic ates his acceptance to the person making the offer then the acceptance must also be communicated to the offer or.

The appellant, a public limited company, was prosecuted for an offence under section 138 of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court convicted him and sentenced him to pay a fine of Rs. 1, 000. On appeal by special leave, the High Court set aside the order of conviction and sentence passed against him on the ground that he had not been given an opportunity to defend himself in the case before the Magistrate. Held, that the order refusing to grant an interim injunction did not determine the rights and obligations of the parties in relation to the matter in dispute in the suit or proceeding. It was not final as it could be said that the decision of the High court was wrong. The question whether the order granting an interim relief should be made absolute or not is a matter which must be decided by the court after hearing the parties.

The respondent company was a manufacturer of processed fabrics and the process or had been manufacturing the processed fabric. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the levy of excise duty on the ground that it was not a'sale'within the meaning of section 2 (f) of the Act, as it did not fall under item No. 1 of the Schedule to the Act. The High Court held that the respondent was not entitled to the exemption under the notification because the goods were manufactured by the process ors and therefore they could not be said to have been sold by them. Dismis sing the appeal, HELD: The respondent is not entitled for the exemption.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk on June 13, 1973. He was promoted to the post of a Head Clerk in January 1974 and he was appointed by the Panchayat Samiti in February 1975. On April 1, 1975, he was promoted as a Head clerk. In March 1975, the appellant was promoted on ad hoc basis to the posts of a head Clerk. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging his appointment as a peon. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant had no right to be considered for promotion to the higher post of Head Clerk. Allow ing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) The appellant's appointment as an Assistant Accountant was not governed by the provisions of the Amending Act of 1973. [ 737 B ] (ii) The appointment of the appellant as a head clerk was not regulated by the Act. It was not bound to absorb him in the post. [ 738 E F ] (iii) The power to make appointments to the Panchayat is vested in the State Government under section 14 (4) of the Act which provides that persons employed by a Panchayat Samiti shall continue to be such officers and servants as may be prescribed. [ 739 C D ] (iv) The word " conditions of service " used in section 14 of the amending Act of 1961 has been interpreted by this Court in the case of State of Haryana vs Shri Ram Kumar,;, followed.

The appellant, a Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowment, filed a suit for declaration that the properties in dispute belonged to the Math Sa una or the deity. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the income from the properties belonging to the temple was not the personal property of the Mahant and that the High court erred in holding that the property was his personal property. Held: (i) The High Court has rightly held that the amount of Rs. 30, 000 which was received by the appellant as the guardian of the trustee of the temple is an income derived from the property of a religious institution. The fact that the appellant had been appointed as the manager of the trust and he was also a member of the committee of management of the said temple does not make any difference. The appellant's claim to exemption from the levy was made under section 2 (1)( d) of the U. P. Agricultural Income Tax Act 1948. The High court was right in holding in favour of the appellant. (ii) The appellant was entitled to exemption only if the income was earned by him from the trust. The income was not taxable because the income could be said to have been earned by the trustee himself. The burden of proof resting on the party who makes the claim was not discharged by the respondent. (iii) The income tax authorities were wrong in holding the income of the assessee as the income derived by the assessee from the endowment. The finding of the High Courts that the expenditure was not incurred by the trustees of the Math and the deity was not correct. (iv) The amount of income from these properties was not income of a person who was not a trustee of a public charitable trust. (v) The amounts of money spent by the devo tees for the purpose of the worship are not income from property of such a nature as would constitute the personal income of an individual.

The appellants were allotted certain lands in the village Rai kot. They filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the allotment of the land to them on the ground that they had been wrongly allotted to the respondents and that their allotment was not in accordance with law. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellants were entitled to the allotment under section 12 (1) of the Act, as they had no right to allotment. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellants that the provisions of section 19 (1), which are similar to sections 10 and 11 of the, could not be applied to the case because the said section did not apply to the present case. Held: (i) The words " any person " in section 10 of the Indian E ase ment Act, 18 91, do not refer to an owner or a managing officer or a manager but only to a managing corporation. The expression'any other law ', in section 2 (d) of that Act, means a law made by Parliament or the Legislature of a State. The word'law'is defined in section 3 (1)( c) of this Act to mean a law relating to the constitution of India. It does not include a law enacted by the legislature of a country. The definition of'law ', therefore, includes all laws which are inconsistent with the Constitution.

The appellants were selected for the post of Upper Primary School Teachers in the State of Uttar Pradesh. They had been appointed as Lower Primary School teachers on the basis of a competitive examination and their selection was made by the Public Service Commission. The recruitment process was completed in two stages, namely, interview and viva voce test. The appellants challenged the action of the Public Services Commission in re suming the recruitment examination and calling them to the interview. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court was wrong in holding that the recruitment process should be stopped because the written examination was not conducted properly and the result of the written test would not have been affected. Dismis sing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The advertisement inviting applications from eligible candidates was published on May 5, 1985 and a corrigendum was published in the newspaper on June 8, 1985. The selection process was started in two phases. The first phase of the recruitment exam is in two parts. The second phase is in the third stage. The third phase is the examination which is in three stages. The examination is in four stages. In the first stage the examination is held in two different stages. There is no justification for cancelling the written part of the Recruitment examin a tion. [ 125 B C ] 2. The Government has taken a decision to cancel the entire recruitment examination. The candidates who are successful in the written examinations are not called for interview but are also provisionally selected. The results of the examination are kept in sealed cover. The respondents are directed to consider the cases of the appellants for appointment as Upper Primary school teachers in the light of the observations made above. [ 126 E F ] 3. The State Public Service Commis sion has decided to cancel all the recruitment examinations and call for fresh interviews. The respondent No. 1 was directed to prepare a fresh list of candidates for the purpose of selection. The appellant's case was that the Public service Commission had not followed the procedure prescribed under the rules. The order of the High court was set aside. [ 127 G H; 128 A ] 4. The question whether the Public Employment Department had committed any mistake in the preparation of the select list or not is a matter which can be considered at the time of final hearing.

The appellant, a member of the D era and its properties, filed a suit against the respondent for recovery of possession of certain properties. The trial court decreed the suit on the ground that the appellant was not a necessary party to the suit and that he had no locus standi to file the appeal. The High Court held that the suit was barred by limitation as it was not instituted within the period prescribed under section 5 (1) of the Code of Civil Procedure. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The High court erred in holding that the appeal was incompetent because the appellant had not impleaded the respondent as a party to it. [ 491 B ] (ii) The appellant could not be added as parties under Order 22, rule 10 of the C. P. C., since the interest of the appellant in the subject matter of the suit devol ved upon him. [ 492 F G ] (iii) The suit was filed on the basis that the plaintiff was not entitled to manage the property of the respondent. The suit should have been filed within the time prescribed under law. [ 493 E ] (iv) The question whether the interest in the property was the subject matters of the litigation or not is a question which can be decided only after evidence has been led by both sides. [ 490 A ] (v) The provisions of Order 22 Rule 10 are not applicable to the present case. [ 494 H;

The petitioners were appointed as Assistant Engineers in the Secretariat of the Andhra Pradesh State Electricity Board. They were promoted to the post of Assistant Engineer on January 9, 1983 and they were confirmed in that post by an order dated October 29, 1979. Their pay was fixed at Rs. 55 per month with effect from February 28, 1983. The petitioners contended that their pay should be fixed at a higher stage than what they had been receiving before the date of their promotion. The respondents contended that the fixation of the age of superannuation was arbitrary and violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. It was further contended that since the Government had not taken into consideration the relevant factors which were relevant for fixing the age limit, it could not have altered the age. Dismis sing the Writ Petitions, ^ HELD: (1) The power conferred by the proviso to Article 309 is of a legislative character and is to be exercised by the Legislature. [ 590 F ] (2) The amendment made to the Fundamental Rules in the exercise of the power conferred under the proviso is of wide amplitude and must be given effect to. [ 591 C D ] (3) The impugned amendments are valid and do not suffer from any infirmity. [ 592 G ] (4) The amended rules cannot be challenged as being ultra vires the Constitution or the Act. [ 593 B ] (5) The amending rules are not open to challenge because they violate Articles 14 and 16 of the constitution. [ 594 E ] (6) The amendments made to Fundamental Rules are valid. [ 595 A ] (7) The provisions of the Fundamental Rule 56 (1)( b) are invalid as they are inconsistent with the fundamental rights guaranteed under Articles 14, 19 and 21 of the Indian Constitution. [ 596 H;

The appellants are dealers in the State of Haryana. They were purchasing raw materials from the manufacturers and selling them to the dealers who, on their own account, sold the manufactured goods to the appellants. The sales were made by the appellants to the respondents at a price higher than the sale price charged by them. The appellants claimed exemption under section 6 (1) of the Act as they had purchased raw materials for the manufacture of goods for export. The assessing authorities held that the purchases were not liable to tax under section 9 but only under section 24 (1). The High Court dismissed the writ petitions filed by the assessees. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the purchase of raw materials by the assessee was not an'input'within the meaning of section 2 (p) of C. S. T. Act, 1956 and therefore, the sales were not exempt under section 5 (1)( b) of that Act. Dismis sing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.
