The purchase of the raw material is not a sale in the hands of the dealer who sells the goods to him. It is not necessary that the goods should be taxed under section 3 or section 6 or section 24. [ 348 A B ] 2. The definition of " turnover " in section 2 sub section (p), read with section 15 of the Central Sales Tax Act, 1948, does not cover the transactions which have been made to the extent of the sales effected by the dealer. The words " goods " in the said section do not include the goods which are actually used for the purpose of export. [ 349 D E ] 3. The expression " goods ", in section 6, means goods other than those specified in Schedule C. Section 6 deals with the goods mentioned in the schedule to the Act. The goods are not specified in the Schedule to the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985. The Explanation to section 6 makes it clear that goods are either to be taxed at the point of purchase or sale. The word " goods'has been defined in section 5 of the C. P. & Ber ar Sales Tax, Act, 1941, as amended by Act No. 23 of 1990. The explanation to section 2 of the said Act provides that goods shall be deemed to have been used in the manufacture thereof for the purposes of the business of any person. [ 350 G H; 351 A ] 4. The term " goods ". in section 3 (i) of Act includes all goods except those specified therein. The proviso to section 24 of the, however, gives an option to the Government to pay tax on the value of the goods. The question whether the goods are taxable in the sense of the term " turnover ", would depend upon the nature of the transaction. If the goods were not sold by the appellant to the respondent, the provisions of section 6 will not apply.

The appellant, a firm registered under the Bombay Sales Tax Act, was assessed to purchase tax on its purchases. The sales were made by it in the course of export and therefore the goods were exempted from payment of tax under section 10 (b) of the Bombay Act. The appellant contended that the goods had been sold to him by the seller and so he could not be said to have purchased them for the purpose of export. Held, that the words " a person " in section 8 (b), must be given their ordinary meaning as they are used in the sense of a person who is not a registered dealer but is a registered assessee. The word " a " in the context means " a registered person ". It is not necessary that there should be an intention to carry out the business of selling goods. The expression " a'is wide enough to include a registered dealers or anybody else. The words " any person " do not mean a registered manufacturer. The fact that the sale is made by a person to whom he sells the goods does not make the sale liable to tax. The mere fact that a person has given such a declaration does not necessarily mean that the transaction is one for the purposes of the Act.

The respondent husband was a divorce e under section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. He filed an application for maintenance in the court of the Magistrate under section 127 (3) of the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973, on the ground that he had been divorced by his wife and that she had no claim to be maintained by him. The Magistrate dismissed the application holding that the respondent was not entitled to maintenance allowance as he had not been given any income from the property. In appeal before the Sessions Judge, the High Court held that the appellant was not a'wife'within the meaning of section 125 (4) of Cr. P. C., but it was a case where the respondent had made a declaration that he was a divorced wife and therefore entitled to the benefit of the provisions of section 127 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925. On appeal, the Division Bench reversed the decision of the trial court and restored the order of the magistrate. Dismis sing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Section 125 (3)( b) is a special provision which must be read with section 127. [ 79 E ] 2. A plain reading of section 126 (3), makes it clear that the legislature intended to give protection to the divorced wife against cruelty or harassment caused to her by her husband during the period of her marriage. It is true that the proviso to section 125 does not make any distinction between the two kinds of cases, but the exception is provided in the context of section 124 (3). [ 80 G H; 81 A B ] 3. The object of the provision is to protect the divorced woman from being deprived of her right to maintenance. The whole scheme of the statute is manifestly to recognise the substitute maintenance arrangement by a statutory or personal law whose quantum is more or less sufficient to do duty for maintenance. [ 82 F ] 4. The word " shall " in section 125 is used in the sense of " may ". The word'shall'has been used in section 127, sub section (3); the words " shall be deemed to have been substituted for the word'may'in section 128 (3 (b) are mandatory. The expression " shall not be so construed as to render it ineffective or redundant " is a reasonable substitute. [ 83 D E ] 5. The language of section 128 is unambiguous and its meaning cannot be de parted from. The phrase ology employed in section 126 is " shall, unless the contrary is proved, be presumed to be correct ". The words " may be " in the section are clear and unambiguous. The words'shall be presumed'are not sy non y mous with the word " may ", and the word ` shall'is not conclusive. The use of the word in the proviso is not decisive. The purpose of the payment'under any customary or personal Law'must be to ob vi ate des titution of the divorce e. [ 84 E F ] 6. The term'shall not ordinarily be construed as'shall '. The word should be interpreted according to the context and the purpose of such interpretation. [ 85 F ] 7. The definition of'shall ', in section 2 (d) of section 2, includes'shall, in relation to the maintenance of a wife, include the provision for maintenance of children. [ 86 B ] 8. The proviso to clause (b), provides that the amount payable to the wife shall not exceed Rs. 500 per month. The amount of maintenance fixed by the Magistrate is not a reasonable addition. The legal character of the amount is not changed. The only just construction of the section is that Parliament intended divorce es should not derive a double benefit.

The appellant was a successful bidder in respect of the contract for sale of liquor. He filed an application before the Collector, Samastipur under Rule 9 (2) of the Bihar Government Servants'Conduct Rules, 1971, alleging that he had been black listed by the State Government and that he was not given any opportunity to make representation against the order. The Collector rejected his application on the ground that there was no requirement in the rule of giving any prior notice before black listing the appellant. The appellant challenged the said order before the High Court. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the order dated 25. 3. 88 was passed without following the rules of natural justice. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the impugned order was bad because the appellant was not afforded any opportunity of making representation against such order. Allow ing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order dated 25th March 1988 is set aside. The matter is remanded back to the Collector with a direction to pass fresh orders after following the PG NO 869 principles of natural Justice. [ 869 E ] 2. The State Government may be directed to pass appropriate orders in accordance with law indicating the reasons therefor.

The appellant, a tenant of the respondent firm, filed an application under section 10 (2)( vii) of the Madras City Ten ants'Protection Act, 1949 for fixation of fair rent in respect of certain premises. The Rent Controller held that the appellant was entitled to relief under the Madras Rent Control Act and directed the eviction of the appellant from the premises. In appeal by special leave, the High Court held that since the landlord had not been able to establish his claim of title to the property, he could not be evicted. On appeal by Special Leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Civil Court had no jurisdiction to determine whether the appellant is a tenant or not. Held: (i) The question as to whether the civil court has jurisdiction to decide the nature or character of the suit properties must be decided by the Rent Controller. If the civil courts have jurisdiction to adjudicate upon the nature of the property which is sought to be taxed, the Civil court will have to go into the question of title. [ 578 C D ] (ii) The expression " any other matter " in section 4 (1) of Act, means only those matters which are expressly excluded from the purview of the Rent Control Legislation. The word " any " in the context of section 4 of the Act cannot be construed to mean a mere reference to the provisions of the statute. It is not possible to accept the contention that the expression " such person " in Section 4 (2) of Madras City Rent Control Acts would include a Court of Small Causes. The words " any person " occurring in section 3 (1), therefore, do not exclude the jurisdiction of the Civil Courts. The expression'any person'in section 2 (e) of Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1948, does not include a person who is not a ry ot or a tenant. The definition of'tenant'in the Act includes a person holding land under a lease or licence. The term'tenant ', in section 5 (1)( b) of that Act, is not defined in the said Act. The meaning of the expression'tenant '. in section 6 (1). is that the person who holds land under another person is not the owner of the land. Therefore, the expression used in section 10 is not confined to a person whose land is being leased out to him but is also covered by the definition of the term'landlord'in that Act. [ 579 E F; G H;

The petitioner was appointed as a Junior Assistant in the Mysore State Civil Service. He was given due opportunity to make his representations against the final list of officers prepared by the Central Government, and he was given an opportunity to file his objections. The petitioner's representation was rejected on the ground that it was not made within the time prescribed under the rules. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the provisional list. The High Court held that the petitioner had no right to challenge the final seniority list. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The petitioner has a right to be heard before the final gradation list is prepared. [ 10 E ] (2) The power of the Courts to interfere with the final lists is always available to the parties concerned. But the question whether the principles are applicable or not depends upon the facts of each case. If the petitioner is aggrieved by the final order passed by the authorities concerned, he can raise all grounds which are open to him. [ 11 F G ] (3) The principle of natural justice cannot be invoked in the matter of fixation of seniority. It is only when there is a possibility of some mistakes occurring about the facts or in the application of the principles governing the equ ation of posts, that the Court may interfere. [ 12 H; 13 A B ] (4) The contention that the petitioners were entitled to have their say in the final select list is untenable. The fact that the respondents were not able to make out a prima facie case for the purpose of fixing the seniority is not sufficient to justify interference with the impugned final list.

The petitioners imported rough di amonds and exported the same under the Import & Export Policy 1978 79. They filed writ petitions in this Court challenging the validity of the said licences on the ground that they were not valid for import of goods as per the Import Policy 1978 80, and that the Additional Lic ences issued to them were invalid because they had been granted additional licences by the authorities concerned. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the petitioners had failed to establish their case that they had made out a case for grant of such exemption. In appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the licence issued to the petitioners was valid for a period of 12 months and that there was no requirement of diver si fication of exports as a condition for grant thereof. Dismis sing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The petitioners have failed to make out a prima facie case for interference by this Court under Article 32 of the Constitution. [ 249 E ] 2. The licences issued to M / s. Suraj Di amonds Industries Pvt. Ltd., are persons similarly situate and therefore, the petitioners cannot claim the benefit of the same relaxation and challenge the validity thereof. [ 250 B C ] 3. The licence issued in favour of M / S. Suraj De i & Co. is valid for the import of items as per para 215 of the Import and Export Policy 1988 91. The order of the Collector of Customs dated April 18, 1985, which has been confirmed by the Appellate Tribunal, is set aside. [ 251 F G ] 4. The petitioner's prayer for interim relief is rejected.

The appellant, a manufacturer of p esticides and packed the goods in bulk and delivered to the customers at their factory. The price charged by them was not included in the assessable value but it was the sole consideration for the sale of the goods. The appellant filed its price lists in respect of the said goods on the basis that they were sold in wholesale as " n aked " and that the price charged was the cost of packing. The Assistant Collector rejected the appellants'claim holding that the appellant had failed to prove that the goods were supplied in a packed condition and that there was no evidence to show that the packing was of dur able nature and was returnable to the buyer. In appeal before the Appellate Tribunal, the appellant contended that (i) the cost incurred by the appellant was not includible in the value of the excisable goods; (ii) the price of the p esticides supplied by the buyer was not the price at which the goods are sold; and (iii) the appellant did not produce any evidence to establish that the p esti cide was sold in bulk or in bulk. Dismis sing the appeals, HELD: 1. 1 The cost of the packing is the cost or value of such packing. It cannot be said that the cost is the price actually paid or payable for the goods when the packing has been supplied by a buyer. [ 10 B ] 2. 1 Section 4 (4)( d)( i) of the Act does not make any distinction between the cost and the price. [ 11 C E ] 2: 2. The cost incurred in the manufacture of p esti o n is not includible. [ 12 D ] 3. 1 There is no question of any addition to the price in respect thereof. [ 13 G ] 3: 2 The cost is not included within the ambit of the price specified in section 4 (1)( b) of Central Excise Act. [ 14 F ] 3 (a) The cost or price of an article is not the sole criterion for determining the value under section 4 of the Central Excise Valuation Act. The value of an item of the same commodity must be determined with reference to the value thereof. If the price is not ascertain able then the cost will have to be added to the assessable price. The fact that the assessee has not produced any evidence in support of his contention that the amount of Rs. 5, 00, 000 /- was not includ able in the price under section 4A (1) of Act, would not make him liable to pay duty. [ 15 H;

The appellant was charged with the offence of criminal conspiracy under section 5 (2) read with section 5. I. P. C. and section 5, Prevention of Corruption Act. The prosecution case was that on the basis of a complaint made by the appellant to the Superintendent of Police, he had taken food from PW 1 for two days and thereafter returned to his house at about 10 p. m. On the same day, the appellant was found in possession of Rs. 100 as bribe. He was arrested and produced before the Magistrate who remanded him to judicial custody. The appellant pleaded not guilty to the charge. The Trial Court convicted him under section 161 I. PC and sentenced him to undergo R. I., for 15 days and also to pay a fine of Rs 500. In appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to one year's rigorous imprisonment. Allow ing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The conviction of the appellant under section 4 (1) of the Prevention of corruption Act is set aside. [ 303 E ] 2. The fact that the appellant had received the money from PW 3, the Principal of the Training School, shows that the explanation offered by the accused was reasonable and probable. It cannot be said that there has been consistent explanation for the appellant. The evidence of PW 1 clearly establishes that the demand was made by PW 1. There was no independent corroboration of the testimony of PW 2 and 6. The recovery of currency notes from the appellant is not supported by any independent evidence.

The petitioner, who was an employee of a company, filed a complaint against the respondents under section 630 (1) of the Companies Act, 1956 alleging that he had been wrongfully obtained possession of certain properties by the respondent and his wife. The Magistrate took cognizance of the offence and issued process to the respondents. The petitioner challenged the order before the High Court in a writ petition which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the expression'any such property'used in cl. (b) of s. 630 (l)( b) includes all assets of a Company as well as its employees. Dismis sing the special leave petition, ^ HELD: (i) The words " any such Property " in cl.( a) are separated from the expression " any other property of the company ". [ 179 D ] (ii) The expression'or'occurring in cl s. (a), (b), (c) and (d) must be read together with the word'or '. It is not necessary that the two expressions should be read harmon iously. The expression " anything " means something more than the ordinary meaning of the word. The word'any'is normally dis jun ctive and con notes a sense of the whole world. The use of the said word may mean either the actual or constructive possession of some thing or the mere fact that it is capable of being so used. [ 180 E F ] (iii) The word " or " in the context in which it appears is used in the sense of a person or persons who has no right to hold property. The term'any property'in cl (a) is used to den ote the property of a particular person or property. If the property is held by a person, the property would be deemed to be the property belonging to him. [ 181 G H; 182 A B ] (iv) The definition of'officer or employee'in section 630 of the Act does not permit the same meaning to be given to the expression. The definition in section 2 (e) of section 630 is wide enough to include any such person or employee.

The appellant was the owner of a temple in the year 18 17. He had been managing the said temple for several years and he was also a member of the public. In the year 19 17, the deity was given by the ancest ors of the appellant who were the devo tees of the temple. The appellant's father died on December 14, 19 17 leaving behind his widow and two sons. The respondent filed an application under section 72 (1) of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950 before the Charity Commissioner, Bombay, praying that the appellant be declared as a public trust under the provisions of the Act. The Assistant Charity Commissioner rejected the application holding that the temple was not a public temple within the meaning of section 2 (13) of Act. On appeal to the District Judge, the High Court held that the Sansthan was a private temple and the appellant was entitled to the declaration that the suit property was a public religious endowment. The High Court dismissed the appeal. Dismis sing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) The appellant is not a person interested in the management of the affairs of the trust. He has no right to do any act which would amount to a public charitable trust. [ 531 B ] (ii) The temple was a religious endowment and its properties were being managed by the public and the deity. The idol was a Hindu public temple. It was a part of the family. The deity was a member thereof. The temple is a public one. The worship per was the only source of income. The ded ication of the property was made by the appellant himself. The entire income from the temple is spent on the services rendered by him. The nature of the endowment is such that it could not be said that the property is a private or public trust. The mere fact that the deity is a religious institution does not make it a private trust. There is no evidence that the object and purpose for which the trust was created, the explicit mode of worship and the object for which it was created are the same. [ 532 F G ] (iii) The deity installed in the temple at Amal ner is a Hindu Religious Trust. The objects and purpose of the Trust are different from those of the Hindu community. The place of worship is a common place of the deity and the worship pers are not merely the acc redited daily pu jar is but also the mul titude of the people who go to the temple for Darshan of the idol. [ 533 C D ] (iv) The idol is a temple. Its worship is not by itself a public or a private one. It is not the case of the respondents that the idol is not an essential part of a public worship.

The assessee was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1943 44 and his total income was Rs. 1, 92, 000. The Income Tax Officer issued a notice under section 13 of the Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 18 76, requiring him to appear before him on the 16th June 1955, but he did not appear. On the 8th July 1955, the Income tax officer issued a warrant of arrest against the assessee under section 14 (2) of the Act. The assessee filed an application in the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution praying that the order of the Income Tax officer be set aside as being without jurisdiction. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the search was illegal because it had been made after the expiry of the period of one year from the date of the seizure and therefore the provisions of section 46 (2)( b) were not applicable. In appeal by special leave, HELD: (i) Section 46 (1) of The Indian Income tax Act, 1922 is valid and does not contraven e article 14 of the constitution. [ 890 G ] (ii) The words " any person " occurring in section 46 are wide enough to include persons who have been subjected to such treatment as may be prescribed by the State Government. It is only when the legislature has chosen to make a law which provides for the levy of a tax or a penalty that the Legislature can do so. [ 891 B C ] (iii) The word " shall " used in section 16 (2), means " shall ". The word'shall'is defined in section 3 (4) of that Act. It includes the power to impose penalties provided in sections 48 and 49. The word ` shall'in section 48 (2). is not restricted to the powers conferred by the Act but is confined to the power of the assessing authority to impose penalty. The power to assess or re assess must be exercised within the four corners of the statute. The expression'shall ', in section 47 (2); cannot be read as meaning'shall '. The word shall'has been used in the context of section 48. [ 892 D E ] (iv) The language of section 47 is clear and unambiguous. The section does not require that the Assessing Authority should be satisfied that the assessee has been guilty of concealment of income or that he has paid up the amount of tax. The provision is intended to provide a remedy for the recovery of the tax. If the assessee fails to pay the tax due within the time fixed, the assessee would be entitled to recover the same. The appellant, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was an industrial undertaking. It was not in existence at the time of its establishment and it was not a factory within the meaning of section 2 (1) of the. The workmen were employed by the appellant as its employees. They had been working for more than nine hours on any day. The appellant's case was that the workmen were not entitled to overtime wages but only to the extent of half an hour's average daily wages. Held, that the Tribunal was right in holding that the appellant was not entitled for overtime wages. The Tribunal was wrong in holding, that there was no provision in the Act or the Rules for payment of overtime wages to the workmen. The provisions of the Act and the Rules made thereunder are not inconsistent with the provisions of any other law. The expression " ordinary rate of wages " means the basic wage plus such allowances including the cash equivalent of the advantages accruing through the concessional sale to the person employed of food grains and other articles as the person engaged is for the time being entitled to but does not include a bonus.

The appellant tenant was a tenant of the respondent landlord. He filed an application for eviction of the appellant tenant on the ground that he had been in arrears of rent from October, 1976 to October, 1977 and therefore it was not possible to pay the amount of rent due by him. The Rent Controller dismissed the application holding that since the premises were let out to the appellant's father the provisions of Section 20 (1) of the Act would apply and therefore the suit could be decreed as the protection under section 20 (2) of Act is not available to the tenant. In appeal before the District Judge, the High Court held that the right of the landlord to evict the tenant under Section 20 of the Rent Control Act was not affected because the proceedings were pending at the time when the Rent Controller passed the decree. On appeal by special leave, the Court, HELD: 1. The rights of the parties will be determined on the basis of the rights available to them on the date of the suit but in accordance with the law applicable to the case. [ 165 A ] 2. The language of Section 40 of the Bombay Rent Act makes it clear that if the provisions contained in this Act are not applicable then no suit shall be instituted except on the specified grounds. [ 166 B C ] 3. The words " any other law " occurring in Section 20 are very wide and must be given their ordinary meaning. It is true that the language of the section does not make it clear whether the legislature intended to exclude the applicability of the provisions which are made in the Act. But the intention of the Legislature is clear that while the provision of the statute is not exhaustive, the provisions should be so interpreted as to give effect to the legislative intent. [ 167 D E ] 4. The object of the enactment is to provide speedy justice to the tenants who have been evicted and to prevent the landlords from being deprived of their property. If the provisions are read in the context of the present case, it is clear, that the purpose of the legislation is to protect the tenants against eviction and not to deprive them of the benefit of the protection afforded by the Rent Act. [ 168 F G ] 5. The expression " any person " in Section 2 (e) of The Act means a person who has been carrying on business or has carried on business in the premises for a long period and has been continuously using the premises in question for a period of 10 years. Therefore, the expression " premises " used in Section 39 of the said Act will not apply for 10 years and therefore so far as the restriction under Section 2 sub clause (2)( a) of Section 2 is concerned, the same cannot be applied for the purposes of the tenancy. [ 169 H;

The appellant, a tenant of the respondent, was in possession of certain lands and was paying rent to the respondent. In the suit for ejectment he claimed that he had been in occupation of the premises as a th ika tenant since 1952 and that he was not entitled to eject him from the said premises. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal the High Court held that the appellant was not liable to ejectment under section 3 of the Act. On appeal by special leave it was contended before this Court that (i) the provisions of the West Bengal Thi ka Tenancy Act, 1949, were applicable to all suits and appeals pending on the date when the Act came into force; (ii) the definition of " th ika tenancy " in section 2 (1)( d) of the Calcutta Thi ka Rent Act, 1948, did not apply to the facts of the case; and (iii) the appellant could not be regarded as a'th ika'tenant within the meaning of the expression'th ata tenant'in section 3. HELD: (i). Section 4 of the Bengal Thi k Tenancy Act 1949, which is a later enactment, does not apply in the present case. [ 185 G ] (ii). The word'th atha'in the Act means a person who has been described as a t ika tenant in the definition clause. It includes any person who is described as such in the section. [ 186 B C ] (iii). The words'th ati or'are not defined in the statute. They have to be construed according to their context and other relevant circumstances. [ 187 F ] (iv) The expression'landlord'in s. 2 (f) of Act of 1949 must mean a person whose land is being used by the landlord for his own use or for the purpose of his business or profession. If the legislature intended to exclude persons who were not so described, then the Legislature would have expressly provided that the expression " th ati " in the latter part of the section would include a person claiming to be a th ati tenant.

The appellant was appointed as a Bench Secretary of the High Court. He was promoted to the post of Bench Secretaries Grade I in the pay scale of Rs. 200 400 and Rs. 500 1200 respectively. On February 1, 1973, he was granted pay scale equal to that of Section Officers. In January 1974, the State Government issued an order dated July 2, 1977 whereby it fixed the pay scales of Section officers with effect from October 1, 1975. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High court challenging the said order on the ground that the same was violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant had been discriminated against by the State. The appeal was allowed. Allow ing the appeal, this Court, HELD: (i) The classification made under the Rules is based on some qualities or characteristics of persons group ed together and not in others who are left out. [ 305 F ] (ii) The principle of " equal pay for equal work " has no mechanical application in every case of similar work. It has to be read into Article l 4 of the constitution. [ 306 G ] (iii) The concept of equality in the matter of pay fixation is a reasonable classification founded on different basis. It is not arbitrary but is based upon intelligible differentia which distinguish es persons group ing together and also bears a rational nexus with the object of differenti ation. [ 307 C D ] (iv) The distinction between the two classes of posts is based solely on the purpose of the exercise of power. The nature of duties and responsibilities of the respective posts have to be determined by experts bodies like Pay Commission, Pay Commissions etc. [ 308 E ] (v) The nature and character of duties, responsibilities and responsibility of each post and the nature of work performed by them are all relevant factors.

The appellant company was a Government Company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956. It had been carrying on business in the State of Uttar Pradesh and it was registered as a dealer under section 65 (d) of the Madhya Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1948. The appellant companies were assessed to sales tax for the period from January 1, 1976 to March 31, 1976. The assessment orders were passed by the assessing authority under the provisions of the U. P. Sales Tax Acts, 1948, which were applicable to the State. The appellants challenged the levy of the tax on the ground that the imposition of the property tax was not authorised by the Central Act but only by the State Legislature. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The power conferred by the Parliament is not in any manner defeated by the legitimate exercise of taxing power under section 69 (d), of the Act of 1973. [ 10 D ] (ii) The State Legislature has no competence to enact the impugned law. The power of taxation conferred by section 127 A of the Municipalities Act is not an independent power. The State legislature has no legislative competence to pass the law on the subject. The powers conferred by sections 129 and 133 of the Municipal Corporation Act are not in conflict with the power conferred on the State Government under section 132 of the said Act. [ 11 C E ] (iii) The question whether the State legislature had the competence to impose the tax or not is a matter of policy. The decision of this Court in Baijnath Ked ia vs State of Bihar & Ors.,;, followed. (iv) The contention that the State Act was not in existence at the time when the power of the State was exercised by the Union Government cannot be accepted. [ 12 G H ] (v) The expression " any other law " in section 2 (g) of U. T. Act means any enactment, ordin ance, regulation, order, bye law, rule, scheme, notification, order or bye law made or issued thereunder. The word'law'in section 3 (d)( i) of that Act includes any enactment relating to the imposition or collection of taxes. The definition of'land'in the Act is wide enough to include all lands and buildings within the meaning of the expression'land '. The expression'building'is defined in section 4 (e) of Act No. 26 of 1975. Section 2 (h) defines'building ', as meaning any building or part of a building which is used or intended to be used for the purpose of a business or profession. The term'building " is defined by section 2 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, which reads as follows: " 2. Definitions.- In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires,- (a) " building " includes a house, shop, hut, shed, wall, hut or other structure, whether of m ason ry, bricks, wood, mud, metal or any other material whatsoever; (b) " prescribed " means prescribed by rules made under this Act; (c) " owner " includes the occupier of a factory; (d). " Prescribed " means the prescribed by Rules made under the Act; and (e). " Form " means a form appended to these rules.

The appellant, a lessee of the Government of Madras, was granted a lease for five years in respect of certain lands. In the year 1942, he applied to the Collector for confirmation of his lease under r. 47 of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1949. He also applied for renewal of the lease on the ground that the land had been leased out to him by the Government and that the appellant's application for renewal was not considered by the Collector. The appellant thereupon filed an appeal before the Board of Revenue which dismissed it. On appeal, the Board held that the lease was valid and that there was no question of the appellant being entitled to the benefit of the second proviso to cl. (iii) of r. 4 of the Abolition Act. Held, that the first proviso to r. 5 (1) of the Regulation did not apply to the case because the appellant had not made any application for the grant of the mining lease under the second Proviso to r., 7 (2). The second proviso was not applicable to the facts of the present case as the appellant was not given an opportunity to show cause against the proposed termination of the leasehold rights.
